📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.
  • It has been revealed that openAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches.
  • We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.

It has been revealed that openAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test⁠(opens in a fresh window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

It has been revealed that testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Industry observers note that shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

Recent findings suggest that shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:.

In a recent development, live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

According to recent reports, defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

It has been revealed that hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

In a recent development, the Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window).

It has been revealed that shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Industry observers note that our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to rapidly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

Industry observers note that we will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

According to recent reports, openAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart⁠(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a latest window).

We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, newly introduced shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window), read the docs⁠(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window).

Around For 'Sunrise On The Reaping' News Noah Schnapp Reveals Image From His 'Sunrise On The Reaping' Audition For Haymitch: "They Picked Right".

Catching Fire still owns the record as Lionsgate’s biggest opening ever at the North American box office.

The running cume through four days on the Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes and Kieran Culkin ensemble.

Before Sunrise on the Reaping, the last big opening for Lionsgate at the domestic box office was 2014’s The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:30PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›.

Billionaire hedge fund manager Stanley Druckenmiller has seemingly turned bearish on stocks, saying recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin that he was largely sitting out of the market and just looking to "not lose money.".

However, while he was a net seller of stocks in Q3, he was quietly adding upcoming positions in three artificial intelligence stocks: Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.35%), Palantir Technologies (PLTR +11.06%), and AppLovin (APP +7.36%).

Let's look at what may have attracted Druckenmiller to these three AI stocks.

Space Exploration Technologies — or SpaceX — is an exciting stock, with the potential to disrupt multiple industries and see rapid growth. While CEO Elon Musk has made some pretty fanciful predictions, such as the company eventually becoming worth more than Earth itself, that hyperbole doesn't take away from what is ultimately a huge opportunity.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/23/26.

The organization’s biggest advantage at this time is its reusable rocket technology, which it has been testing with its much larger-payload Starship.

In a recent development, with the manufacturer recently catching the upper stage of Starship, it has now demonstrated that it can recapture both stages of the rocket, positioning it for the beginning of rapid rocket reuse. That would completely turn the economics of space on its head and give SpaceX an enormous cost advantage not only for launching more Starlink satellites but also for the future launch of orbital data centers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were unveiled in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

In a recent development, the idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the newly introduced version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:.

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Sources indicate that before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

In a recent development, that’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

According to recent reports, the only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Sources indicate that have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that type-C is C11 with the types C is missing: variants that match checks, distinct types for ids and units, generic types, and errors as values with try and defer.
  • Type-C is early: every example on this page works today, and the rest of the language is designed but not built yet (Status).
  • Homebrew builds typec from the release source with OCaml and dune.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that type-C is C11 with the types C is missing: variants that match checks, distinct types for ids and units, generic types, and errors as values with try and defer. Its compiler, typec, takes the command line of cc, turns Type-C into C that you can read, and hands that C to your C compiler. A C11 file is already a Type-C file, so a program adopts it one file at a time.

Type-C is early: every example on this page works today, and the rest of the language is designed but not built yet (Status).

With Homebrew, on macOS or Linux:.

Homebrew builds typec from the release source with OCaml and dune. typec hands its C to cc unless told otherwise (Choosing the backend). To build it from a checkout instead, see Try it.

Sources indicate that an evaluator of arithmetic expression trees, which reports a division by zero or an overflow as a value instead of crashing. Like every C and Type-C example in this README, it is checked by the tests.

It builds with the options of cc and prints:.

What Type-C adds to C explains each new piece, and indicates the mistakes each one rules out. The tutorial grows a C program into Type-C one feature at a time, and the language reference states the rules of each construct.

Each feature below rules out a kind of mistake that C compiles without a word: as an error that the section shows, or by making the mistake impossible to write. Where a C warning catches a form of it, the section claims which. The messages are those that typec prints, with its exit status in brackets (What typec reports). The cases of a variant are its constructors, as the messages call them.

A tagged union in C, with two bugs:.

The same in Type-C. Each field belongs to its case, so the wrong-member read cannot be written, and the forgotten case stops the build:.

C's -Wall warns of a forgotten enumerator only in a switch with no default, and only when the kind has an enumeration type; a default written for a kind that is none of the three, or an int kind, hides it (-Wswitch-enum warns with the default too). No flag that test/run/comparison.t tries warns of the wrong-member read. A match needs no default: it stops the program on a value whose tag is none of the cases, and a case added later is an error at every match that misses it.

if (case ...) tests for one case and binds its fields, and while (case ...) loops while it holds. Outside them and match, Type-C code cannot name a field at all:.

A field read as C reads a member of the union:.

An arm of a match that can run into the next one is an error: it ends in break, return, continue, goto or a call that does not return.

In C, GCC's -Wextra warns of a missing break, and Clang does with -Wimplicit-fallthrough.

A distinct type has the representation of another type but does not convert to it, or from it, without a cast. Ids and units that C would mix become an error:.

With C's typedef, the swap compiles, and no warning flag that comparison.t tries catches it:.

An interface file, .tci, is a header for Type-C: other files include it with #include. A private type in it can be made only in the interface and in the source file of the same name, here port.tc; other files use ports and read their value. So, short of C code or reinterpreted storage (limits), every port but the zero value, {0}, comes from port_parse.

Recent findings suggest that A type can take type parameters, instead of holding a void *. list(int) and list(double) are different types, so a list of prices cannot reach a function that sums integers. Each list(int) names the same type, wherever it is written.

Each instance of a generic type is a C structure of its own, and a structure converts to no other type, so typec refuses list(double) where list(int) is wanted:.

The C list of void * takes any element:.

option(T) is a generic variant that every Type-C file has: None, or Some of a value. It replaces the -1 or NULL that means "not found", which a caller can forget to test:.

result(T, E) is another generic variant that every Type-C file has: Ok of a value, or Err of an error, which can be a variant with fields of its own. try gives the value of a result, or returns its error from the function at once:.

A call that drops a result, as a statement of its own, is an error:.

C drops a return code without a word unless its function is declared [[nodiscard]] (C23) or warn_unused_result, and then it warns.

C releases resources at one label that each error path must jump to; here an error path written later returns past it:.

Industry observers note that A defer, written on the line after an acquisition, releases the resource at every exit after it: each exit runs the deferred statements in force there, in reverse order, so the return in the loop closes both files. A deferred statement cannot report an error, so the function flushes out itself before its last exit:.

In a recent development, typec writes a copy of each deferred statement at each exit (What the C looks like). An analyzer finds some leaks of C by following paths: GCC's -fanalyzer reports both of copy.c, in either order.

Industry observers note that A match with a default covers a new case as C's default does; but a default that covers no case is refused, so one cannot be written "just in case" before the case exists. A value whose tag is none of its cases, which C code, casts and unions can make, stops the program when it is matched, at run time. private binds Type-C files only: C code reads and writes the layout as C does, the zero value is open to every file, and Type-C code that reinterprets storage, as *(port *)p does, is not refused. The guarantees and what each depends on are in design 14.

Type-C enters a program one file at a time. Take a small C program: main.c calls calc.c through calc.h.

Industry observers note that calc.c becomes calc.tc, which parses a line into a variant and matches on it. It still includes calc.h, and calc_apply keeps its C type, so main.c and calc.h do not change:.

Sources indicate that typec compiles calc.tc to an ordinary object. The C compiler links it with the main.o of the C build, which is not even recompiled:.

A command added to command later, such as Mul(long n), stops the build at every match that does not handle it.

A build compiles calc.tc with typec, and its other files as before (In a build).

A C11 translation unit is a Type-C unit with the same meaning (design 2.2): each Type-C construct begins with tokens that C refuses, and the words Type-C adds, such as type, match and result, stay free for C's identifiers (design 2.3). So a file renamed to .tc compiles before any Type-C is written in it, and while it uses no Type-C construct, typec hands the C compiler its preprocessed text byte for byte: the object equals the one that the C compiler builds from that same preprocessed text with the same options (test/run/pipeline.t). The corpus runner checks the same on every file of real programs, among them zlib, Lua, SQLite and QBE, each renamed to .tc (Running the corpus); recording a run of the whole corpus at one revision on every host is open in TODO.md.

The fine print, for a .tc file:.

Recent findings suggest that the code that you write in Type-C compiles to plain C (What the C looks like). Of the code that the compiler adds without the source spelling it out, the traps of matching, the cleanups of defer and slice bounds checks are built; checked mode will add the rest (principle 4). The rest of a program links as before: Type-C functions are C functions under their own names, with no mangling, and typec adds no library to the link (design 10.4). Debuggers step through the lines of the .tc file (design 13.6), but the debug information is not yet that of a direct compile: with Clang it names a temporary file as the compilation unit, and on macOS a command that links a .tc input with other inputs loses the .dSYM of -g (TODO.md).

In a build, typec is the C compiler, with the backend that TYPEC_CC names (Choosing the backend). It hands main.c and every other C file to the backend untouched, so a build tool needs to learn only that a .tc file is compiled as a .c file is. The dependency options (-M, -MM, -MD, -MMD, -MF, -MT, -MQ, -MP) work as for a .c file: the rule of calc.o names calc.tc and every header and .tci interface that it includes, so make or ninja rebuilds calc.o when one of them changes, and nothing when none does.

In a GNU Makefile, the rule for a .tc file is make's built-in rule for a .c file:.

With ninja, whose deps = gcc reads the same dependency files:.

In CMake, a file of rules that CMake reads when it enables C makes .tc a suffix of C sources:.

The LANGUAGE C property on calc.tc would not do: with it, CMake puts -x c before the file, and typec then hands it to the backend as C, as the C compiler would take it. The tests make_rule.t, ninja_rule.t and cmake_rule.t build with these rules on both backends, where the host has the tool.

typec stops at the first error it finds, prints it as GCC and Clang print theirs, file:line: error: message with the line of the source under it, and exits with status 80. The line has no caret: the C compiler preprocesses the source, so the error names a line and no column (design 13.6). An error under a rule of Type-C ends with the rule's name in brackets, as [match-arm-end], the way GCC ends a warning with its option; the catalogue of diagnostics (dune build docs/diagnostics.md writes it to _build/default/docs/diagnostics.md) gives each name's rule and the section of the design that states it. A message about no place in the source, as one about the command line, begins with typec: instead. An error that the C compiler finds in the C that typec writes, as with the generic types above, comes with the C compiler's message and status. test/run/readme.t checks the files and the output of every C and Type-C example on this page, on GCC and Clang.

It has been revealed that typec writes plain C11 with the GNU extensions that GCC and Clang share, and --emit-c prints it. A variant is a structure of an enumeration, its tag, and a union of one structure for each case that has fields. The enumeration ends with a hidden enumerator of the value INT_MAX, so the tag has the size of int with or without -fshort-enums. A match is a switch on the tag that copies the fields an arm binds into const locals, and traps after each arm and in the default that it adds for a tag that is none of the cases, beside the case of the hidden enumerator. A C switch on a tag needs a default too, or -Wswitch reports that enumerator. A distinct type is a typedef of the type it is made from, and an instance of a generic type is a structure named after its arguments, as list__i is list(int). C code and Type-C code call each other with no glue. C text that uses no Type-C construct is written out as it was read.

typec --emit-c shape.tc writes this, here without its line markers and laid out for reading:.

The unit ends with a few static assertions of what typec assumes of the target, which fail to compile where the C compiler's types differ from those typec read, as under a wrapper that adds -funsigned-bitfields.

A result is a variant like any other, an instance named after its arguments, as result__i5error is result(int, error). A try tests the tag and returns the error at once, and a defer writes its statement at each exit of its scope, in reverse order, after the value of a return is computed: the C of early returns that each release what is held, with no table, unwinding or allocation.

typec --emit-c pair.tc writes this, here without its line markers and laid out for reading:.

A tag that is neither Ok nor Err traps, as in every match, and so does the end of the function, which no path reaches.

According to recent reports, the lowering is measured against hand-written C: Type-C programs and C twins of them, which carry the same checks (the trap of a match on a bad tag, the copies of the bound fields), are built at -O2 with both compilers and compared in code size and in the instructions they retire (Measuring against hand-written C). The cost of the checks themselves, and what is not measured yet, are open in TODO.md.

Recent findings suggest that C code sees what design 10.6 lists: a variant is the structure shown above, a distinct type is the type it is made from, and a function is the same C function. The C compiler lays out both sides, so they agree: test/run/abi.t links objects that typec builds with objects of the C compiler alone, in every pairing of GCC and Clang, and passes variants with fields of each class of C object type both ways, the C side reading them through a structure written by hand as design 10.1 gives it.

Recent findings suggest that one header can serve both kinds of file. typec defines __TYPEC__ while it preprocesses a Type-C unit, so the header can give Type-C files a distinct type where C files see a plain typedef (design 2.1). Both have the same representation, so both call the same function, and only the Type-C side gets the check:.

typec --emit-c-header M.tci writes M.h, the C header of a .tci interface, so that C code gets its variants without a structure written by hand (design 9.3). A Type-C unit that includes M.h reads M.tci itself. The dependency options work as for a .tc file, with the header as the target of the rule, which names M.tci and every file that it includes: -MD and -MMD write the rule to M.h.d, the header's path followed by .d, or to the file that -MF names, so a makefile rule M.h: M.tci whose command is typec --emit-c-header -MMD -MP M.tci, with -include M.h.d beside it, rebuilds M.h when an interface that M.tci includes changes. -M and -MM print the rule, or write it to the -MF file, and write no header, so they cannot be used with -o. Under -o - no path names the header, and -MD and -MMD need -MT or -MQ and -MF.

Industry observers note that pilot B, the initiative's test of Stage 2 on real code (plan, Stage 2), rewrote the parser of tomlc99, a TOML library in C (toml.c, 2392 lines), with result, try and defer. Its header toml.h, its C programs and its tests did not change and link against the Type-C object. The pilot's repository is not published; the numbers here are from its record.

Sources indicate that fault injection fails each allocation of a parse in turn, one run for each. Over the library's 62 example files, 1416 runs, the original went wrong in 34: 25 leaks and 9 uses after free, from two defects in the code that grows an array or a table. The rewrite went wrong in none, built by Clang or GCC, and the address, undefined behavior and leak sanitizers reported nothing. Over the 146 files of toml-spec-tests, 18847 runs, the original leaked in 1022, 1000 of them in one deeply nested file, and crashed in 9; the rewrite did neither.

try and defer did not remove the defects by themselves. A variant of the rewrite whose three faulty functions only put a try in place of each if (!x) return kept all 34 bad runs. Adding a defer that frees each new object until it is linked into the tree removed the 25 leaks but not the 9 uses after free, which came from the order of the steps: the old buffer of an array was freed before its new element existed. Reordering the steps, so that each grown buffer is stored and counted before the next allocation, removed them. The language puts the question "who owns this object if this step fails?" at every try; the rewrite had to answer it.

What it costs, at -O2 -g, against a hand-written C version of the same rewrite with a goto cleanup where Type-C has a defer:.

The record does not split the rest of the growth further and puts most of it down to the representation of result, a structure of a tag and a union returned by value where the C returns an int or a pointer; returning a result whose error has no fields as the bare value is open in TODO.md. Parse times are the best of five rounds, and repeated runs move each by 2 to 3 percent, more than any gap between the versions. Error paths were not timed.

One line each on the principles of design section 1, which states them in full:.

...turn on more warnings, or run an analyzer? Use them: Type-C code still gets the warnings of the C compiler. Warnings see only the forms they were written for, and no flag that comparison.t tries catches a read of the wrong member, swapped ids or a value made outside its module. An analyzer finds what the paths it explores reach. In Type-C these mistakes are type errors that every build checks, with no extra tool.

It has been revealed that ...use Rust, Zig or OCaml? All three have tagged unions whose matches are checked for missing cases, and generic types, and safe Rust and OCaml are memory safe, which Type-C is not (design 14). All three call C, but C code gains their checks only when it is rewritten in their language, and the build gains their toolchain and a boundary between the languages: Rust reads C's declarations through extern "C" blocks, written by hand or generated by bindgen, Zig translates C headers into Zig, and OCaml calls C through stubs written against its runtime, which brings a garbage collector. typec is a tool to add too, but in Type-C the checks start in the one file you rename. It includes the same headers as they are, is compiled by the same C compiler, and gives an object with the C ABI, which links with the rest as before (Adopting one file).

...use C++? std::variant, enum class and templates do much of this, in another language. A C file is not always a C++ file (int *p = malloc(n); is an error in C++), C++ reaches C functions through extern "C" declarations, and C++ brings exceptions and a runtime library to link. A C file stays valid Type-C, and typec writes C.

...write macros? A macro that writes struct { T *data; ... } makes a new type at each use, so the VECTOR(int) of one declaration does not pass where another VECTOR(int) is wanted, and C refuses the call. The usual fix declares each instance once by name, by hand. A generic type such as vector(int) is one type wherever it is written. A macro cannot check a switch either.

Type-C 1.0 is the core language, frozen: variants, match, if (case ...) and nested patterns, distinct types, private and interface files (.tci), generic types and functions, option and result, try and defer, and slices with checked indexing and str. typec --emit-c-header writes the C header of an interface for C clients. The design specifies the whole language, and the plan built it in stages, each ending in a measured gate, and the three pilots build with this release (Measured on a real library).

The test suite passes with Clang and with GCC on macOS, x86-64 and arm64, and on Linux, with glibc on x86-64 and with musl on x86-64 and arm64 (Building and testing).

Designed and not yet implemented: a checked mode, whose rules are provisional, that rules out specific classes of memory errors in the functions it covers (Stage 5 of the initiative).

It has been revealed that you need OCaml, dune and a GCC or Clang, of the releases that Building and testing names. From a checkout, with the examples above saved under their names:.

typec takes the command line of cc and hands an input that is not a .tc file to the C compiler untouched, so an existing build runs with CC=typec and its C files compile as before. With a .tc input it refuses the few options that it cannot follow, such as -E, which stops before the C it writes, or -funsigned-bitfields, which changes C's types, and the long options, spelled with --, that it does not know. The C compiler is cc unless --cc=PATH or TYPEC_CC names another (choosing it).

examples/ holds larger programs, each beside the C that it ports, such as FreeBSD's cut(1).

Requirements: OCaml 5.4 and dune 3; the tests also need a C compiler as cc, a Clang and a GCC of releases that typec supports (see Choosing the backend), and tools/corpus/runner.t runs /usr/bin/clang. The cram tests in test/run run the Clang that TYPEC_TEST_CLANG names and the GCC that TYPEC_TEST_GCC names; unset, they are /usr/bin/clang and the gcc-16 on the PATH, those of a macOS host with Homebrew's GCC (test/run/backends.sh). headers.t parses and reads the declarations of every C11 and POSIX header that each backend's system headers hold. target.t expects the model of x86-64, of arm64 Linux or of arm64 macOS, and types.t, declarations.t and expressions.t compile for the host's target and for a second one, -m32 on x86-64 and the other signedness of plain char elsewhere (second_target in test/run/backends.sh). A host without the C headers of i386 runs the tests that include the C headers (abi.t) with the other signedness of plain char instead of -m32, and dune test prints a line saying so. A host that has them sets TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_M32 to a non-empty value, and dune test then fails when the backends do not both compile with -m32; the check is a rule of test/run/dune, so a run of one test alone (dune test test/run/abi.t) skips it. short_enums.t and c_header.t also run the arm-none-eabi-gcc that TYPEC_TEST_ARM_GCC names, or the one on the PATH, where present, and Clang for thumbv7m-none-eabi where Clang has that target. The rule that reports -m32 also prints which of the two Arm backends ran and which were skipped, and fails when one is missing and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_ARM is set to a non-empty value. tutorial.t runs its lldb examples where the lldb on the PATH debugs the programs of both backends; the same rule prints whether they run on this host, and fails when they do not and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_LLDB is set to a non-empty value. The sanitized tests add AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer on each backend that links them; the rule prints whether each backend does, and fails when one does not and TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_SANITIZERS is set to a non-empty value. There are no other dependencies.

dune exec typec -- ARGS runs the compiler from the build tree.

Industry observers note that tools/gate.sh is the command to run before a commit: it runs dune build, dune build @check and dune test, then builds the typing oracle and runs its tests, which dune test skips (see Typing oracle). It needs the opam switch tools and fails, saying where to find how to create it, when the switch is missing. Before its steps it prints that report, which dune test writes only to the log, so a skipped Arm backend shows, and stops where a TYPEC_TEST_REQUIRE_* variable of test/run/backends.sh names one that is missing. It prints the end of the log when a step fails; the variables in the header of the script set the opam root, the oracle's build directory and the log.

Library tests are in test/unit; the parser's are tables of C text and the structural dump of its tree (test/support/tree_dump.ml) or its error. test_deep_trees runs every chain that the parser reads in a loop (test/support/chains.ml), as deep as Parser.max_depth lets it, through the stages after the parser on a stack limited to 256K words of amd64 frames (more where a frame is larger). test/golden holds cram tests that show the C or the diagnostic that the front end gives for a source, with no backend (test/golden/golden.ml); dune test test/golden runs them and dune promote takes a changed output. Every rule that typec enforces has a stable name in the one table src/syntax/rule_table/rule_table.ml, which generates the module Rule and the catalogue _build/default/docs/diagnostics.md (dune build docs/diagnostics.md); test/golden/coverage.ml fails while some rule's name appears in no golden output, so a newly introduced rule needs a golden case, and test/golden/citations.ml fails while an expected output of a golden or run test states the word "design": a diagnostic says what is wrong in the terms of the user's text, and its rule name is the reference. test/run holds cram tests that run typec and the backends; types.t and declarations.t compile static assertions of what typec computes, so a backend that disagrees fails to compile them. test/misuse holds OCaml that an interface must refuse; each file names its library and the expected error text in a (* misuse: LIBRARY TEXT *) line, and passes only when ocamlc rejects it with that text.

Sources indicate that the backend is the program named by the last --cc=PATH option, else by the TYPEC_CC environment variable when it is set and not empty, else cc. A name without a slash is looked up in PATH. typec consumes --cc=, --print-target, --emit-c, --emit-c-header, --stats, --trap-function= and --version where an option can stand (the value of -o is never one) and forwards every other argument, --cc without = included, in its original order. The backend is run with an argument vector, never through a shell, so TYPEC_CC names one program: it cannot carry extra arguments such as ccache gcc.

A backend that runs typec again, such as a cc first on PATH that is typec itself, is refused: typec sets TYPEC_OUTER_CC to the backend's name in the environment of every backend it runs, and a typec that starts with it set exits with 81 after one message naming that backend. The whole process tree of the backend inherits the mark, so a typec that a wrapper backend runs on purpose is refused too. To install typec as cc, set TYPEC_CC to the path of the real C compiler.

In a recent development, the backend is GCC or Clang, Apple's included, no older than the releases that minimum_major_version in src/sema/target.ml names. typec refuses an older one with a message naming the oldest supported releases.

Without a .tc input typec replaces itself with the backend. Exit status: the backend's own; a backend ended by a signal ends typec with the same signal. typec exits with 81 when --cc= has no path, --trap-function= names no C identifier or one reserved to typec, the backend cannot be started or the backend runs typec again, after one message on stderr (with --print-target, a second indicates that the backend gave no target model).

typec's own failures have statuses of their own, which src/driver/exit_status.ml defines and design 13.2 explains: 80 when it refuses the program (a diagnostic about the source), 81 for an error of its environment (the command line, the backend, a file it cannot read or write) and 82 for an internal error, a bug in typec. Every other status is the backend's.

An input whose name ends in .tc, with no -x other than -x none before it, goes through three steps:.

In a recent development, on Clang, steps 1 and 3 also get -Wno-unused-command-line-argument before OPTIONS, so that Clang does not warn about an option of the command line that the step does not use. GCC does not know the option, so its steps go without it. The query for the target model runs before the backend is known and gets it on both.

-std=gnu17 is left out when the command line gives -std= for C11 or C17 (c11, c17, c18, gnu11, gnu17, gnu18, c1x, gnu1x, iso9899:2011, iso9899:2017, iso9899:2018); any other -std= is a usage error. Step 2 reads asm and typeof as keywords in the GNU forms and as identifiers in the ISO forms, as GCC and Clang do; -fasm and -fno-asm select the GNU and the ISO keywords whatever -std= claims. The options of step 1 are those that matter to preprocessing and to code generation, those of step 3 the latter only; src/driver/cc_option.ml is the one table that tells them apart and says which options take a separate value. The output is named as cc names it: after -o, else after the input in the current directory. When the command line links and has no input but .tc ones, step 3 is the final command: the backend compiles and links the command line with each .tc input replaced by -x cpp-output EMITTED, where EMITTED is named as the input with the suffix .c, in a directory of its own. The backend thus leaves what it leaves for a one-step build of C sources, named as there: on macOS the .dSYM bundle of -g, and the files of -gsplit-dwarf, -fstack-usage and -fcallgraph-info. When the command line links with other inputs, each .tc input becomes an object in the temporary directory and the backend links the command line with those objects in place of the .tc inputs, and the side outputs of step 3 are lost with the objects; without linking, the other inputs are compiled by one more backend command without the .tc inputs. A .c input is thus compiled exactly as without typec.

It has been revealed that with -MD or -MMD the dependency file comes from step 1, named as cc names it: after -MF, else after -o with the suffix .d, else after the input; its target is the -MT or -MQ value, else the real output. With -M or -MM the command line compiles nothing: step 1 of each .tc input prints its rule in place of the preprocessed text, to the -o file or stdout, and one more backend command gets the command line without the .tc inputs, when other inputs remain, to print theirs.

--emit-c stops after step 2 and writes the C to the -o file, or to stdout; the command line then has exactly one input, a .tc file.

Sources indicate that --trap-function=NAME makes every trap of the emitted C (a corrupted tag, a slice index out of range) call _Noreturn void NAME(void), which the program supplies, instead of executing __builtin_trap() alone; a freestanding program uses it to report the failure (design 10.5). NAME is a C identifier of ASCII letters, digits and underscores outside the names reserved to typec, which begin with __tc_, and the last --trap-function= wins. NAME is the name the program defines, not a macro: the emitted C is already preprocessed, so -DNAME=... does not change it. A .tc unit that holds a Type-C construct declares NAME after its own text, so a declaration of NAME in the program with another type is a backend error reported at typec's text ().

--stats prints on stderr, for each .tc input and for the .tci input of --emit-c-header, one line typec: stats: FILE: and the fields unit_bytes (the preprocessed unit), instance_bytes (charged to the instance budget), copy_bytes (the front end's charge to the output limit for the copies of deferred statements, which output_bytes counts again), output_bytes (charged to the output limit by lowering, the unit's own text included, and for a header then every byte of the header, its macro brackets and macro probe among them), output_limit, longest_instance_code (the most bytes of the code of one instance, its generic's name and the encodings of its arguments, that the bound on encodings holds) and longest_name (of a type declaration or a generic function, the universe text included), each as name=value: the counts of design 3.5 rule 7 that the measurements of P30 read. Then come the slice tests of the unit and of each instance that it uses, which the measurements of P28 read: slice_indexes, slice_subs and slice_conversions (those that C evaluates, which lowering writes with a test), slice_untested (those that C does not evaluate) and slice_late_calls (the tested indexes and slice_subs with a call or a statement expression in an operand after the first). Last come the most steps (selection_steps), nodes (selection_nodes) and nodes on one path (selection_depth) that building the selection tree of one match or test of the unit or of an instance took, which the measurements of P32 read, each the most over all of them. The holders of a try of the unit and of each instance come last, which the measurements of P33 to P35 read: try_holders (the holders), try_tries (their try expressions), try_first_operands (the hoisted operands that are the first operand of &&, || or a conditional operator or the left operand of a comma), try_conditioned (the hoisted operands under a condition) and try_multiple (the holders with more than one hoisted operand). A unit that typec refuses reports none.

A .tc input refuses the option that stops the backend at preprocessing (-E), the options that change the preprocessed text (-P, -C, -CC, -fuse-line-directives, -traditional-cpp, -fdirectives-only), every -d option of dumps (-dD, -dM, -dI and the like), alone or passed on by -Wp,, -Xpreprocessor or -Xclang (which so refuses Clang's -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone too), -save-temps, -###, -ansi, --, the options that name a file of further options (response files, @FILE, -specs= and --config=) and the queries that print a fact of the backend (-print-file-name= and every other -print- option, -dumpmachine), with a usage error naming the option. It refuses a long option, spelled with --, that it does not know, as GCC reads --NAME as -fNAME and accepts abbreviations, so that --preprocess, --write-user-dep or --short-enums cannot reach the backend unseen; an option that also has a form with one - passes in that form. It refuses the options known to change a type of C without changing a macro that the target model reads, which the model therefore cannot see: -funsigned-bitfields or -fno-signed-bitfields, and -fsingle-precision-constant, even when a later option undoes them. -fshort-enums passes: the target query learns the enumeration representation by its probe compiles (Printing the target model). Other routes to these types, such as a config file, a wrapper or a target whose default differs, fail in step 3: the C of a unit with a Type-C construct ends, after a line marker for with flag 3, with a static assertion of each such type that typec assumes, whose message names the option that would break it; that of the enumeration rule also states the representation that typec expects. Flag 3 keeps the user's warning options off typec's own text. An option that changes a macro the model reads, such as -funsigned-char or -fshort-wchar, reaches the target model. It refuses -fpack-struct without a value, under which GCC ignores the #pragma pack lines that typec writes around an instance of a generic and warns of each; -fpack-struct=n passes. A unit that holds such lines also ends with a probe that fails where the backend reads #pragma pack() as a pop, as Clang does under -fapple-pragma-pack. It also refuses -arch options that name more than one architecture: cc builds a universal binary from them, but step 1 preprocesses for one architecture only. Build each architecture with its own -arch and join the results with lipo -create.

A freestanding build passes -ffreestanding -nostdlib as for C. The objects need from the environment what the same C needs, such as memset, and nothing more: a trap is __builtin_trap(), an instruction on x86-64 and AArch64 (design 10.4).

It has been revealed that the temporary directory is made with mode 0700 in TMPDIR, or /tmp, and removed on every way out. SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGPIPE, SIGQUIT and SIGTERM are passed on to the running backend; typec then removes the directory and ends by the same signal.

Exit status: 0 when every step succeeds; else the status of the first backend step that fails, or the signal that ended it; 80 when the reader or the front end refuses the preprocessed text; 81 for a usage error, when the backend cannot be started or gives no target model, or when a file cannot be read or written; 82 for an internal error.

typec --print-target [OPTIONS] runs the backend as BACKEND OPTIONS -dM -E -x c /dev/null and prints the target model that its predefined macros give: the backend and its major version, the sizes of the scalar types, the signedness of char, the types behind size_t and the other standard typedefs, the byte order and __STDC_VERSION__, one field: value per line, and last the enumeration representation, int-sized or short (as under -fshort-enums), which no macro states: typec learns it by two compiles of a probe, BACKEND OPTIONS -fsyntax-only -w -dumpdir DIR/ -x c -, each of which compiles under one representation alone. Whether the backend has __float128, among the optional floating types, comes from a third compile of the same form, since no macro claims so on every target. The other arguments are the backend options that select the target or the dialect, such as -m32, -funsigned-char or -std=gnu17; inputs, -o and dependency options do not belong there.

Exit status: 0 with the model on stdout; 81 when the backend fails, cannot be started, is not supported or prints macros the model cannot be read from, when it compiles neither probe or both, or for a usage error; 82 for an internal error.

Recent findings suggest that typec --version runs BACKEND --version, passes on its output, then prints typec and its release on a last line, such as typec 1.0. A build tool that tells compilers apart by the output of $CC --version, such as Meson, or a script that reads its first line thus sees the backend. The rest of the command line does not reach the backend and nothing is compiled, as GCC and Clang compile nothing with their --version; an error in one of typec's own options, such as --cc= without a path, is still one. The status is the backend's, or 81 when it cannot be started, or 0 when SIGPIPE ended the backend and the reader of the output is gone, as a reader such as head -1 that stops early is no failure; a backend that fails or cannot be started is named on stderr, and typec's line is still printed. The release has one source, the version field of dune-project, which the build writes into typec; a release tag vX.Y is made after it is set.

docs/typec.1, in mdoc(7), is installed by dune install as man/man1/typec.1 under the prefix, or under the directory of --mandir. test/unit/test_manual.ml checks its lists of typec's options and exit statuses against the driver's tables, and mandoc -Tlint -Wwarning docs/typec.1 checks its markup.

According to recent reports, the test hosts, fuzzing, the corpus runner, the typing oracle and the measurements against hand-written C are described in docs/development.md. The order of work is the implementation proposal, and open work is in TODO.md.

HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • In a recent development, A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

In a recent development, A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

In a recent development, “Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

Industry observers note that in the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

Sources indicate that it’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that although Black Friday is still a few days away, the deals are already filtering in. If you're after a new mechanical keyboard — maybe your first, maybe your 10th, or if you're anything like me, maybe your 50th — this is easily the best time of year to get one.

It has been revealed that I'm Pete. I've reviewed dozens of mechanical keyboards, tested and owned dozens more, and edited hundreds of keyboard reviews from my team. At the risk of sounding my own horn, I'm a keyboard expert. So I follow pricing throughout the year.

In a recent development, I've rounded up some of my favorite early Black Friday keyboard deals here. My top pick is the Keychron C2 Pro 8K, now just $48 at Amazon — it offers nearly unparalleled value for money. There are plenty more deals where that came from, though. All these boards have been tested personally by me or my team, and they all scored high — to do that, by definition, they had to be excellent to type on.

Cute and compact, we gave the Logitech Pebble Keys 2 our Recommended badge and 4 coveted stars in our review. Circular keycaps might not be for everyone, but this will still certainly be an upgrade over a crappy work keyboard or tired laptop keyboard.

This keyboard practically defines value for money. We tested the 80% variant, the Keychron C1 Pro 8K, which is essentially the same board without a num pad. It offers excellent typing and solid gaming performance, too. And now for under $50.

My first mechanical keyboard was the Keychron K2, so it holds a special place in my heart. This is an excellent starter keyboard for a first time mechanical user. This variant isn't hot-swappable like the C2 Pro above, so the C2 is better if you want to customize your board. However, if you're after a more compact 75% layout, I heartily recommend the K2.

In a recent development, I awarded this board a full five star score in my Keychron V6 review. If typing is your main priority and you don't need the gaming features of the C2 Pro, the V6 is incredible value for money. It's also designed to be a starting point for custom builds, as you can fully take it apart, so great for newcomers to the custom scene — you can experiment with modding but not drop too much cash.

It has been revealed that I loved this board in my Lofree Flow Lite review. In typical Lofree style, it's beautiful to behold, oozing minimalist charm. Thanks to Lofree's long-running partnership with switch manufacturer Kailh, you're also getting some of the best switches on the market for typing. Hardcore typists who need a portable, low-profile deck: this one's for you.

Sources indicate that fancy adding some fun to your desk? The Gravastar Mercury K1, which we gave four stars, never fails to turn heads. While I didn't review it personally (our writer Nikita did), I used this as my main gaming keyboard for several months at home. It types and sounds absolutely gorgeous. (macOS users be warned, this deck only really works properly on Windows or Linux.).

It has been revealed that our staff writer Nikita (the only person on our team to have reviewed more keyboards than me!) gave the Epomaker Glyph our Editor's Choice badge in her review. Despite having the pick of literally any keyboard she could choose, she still uses this as her daily work driver. So yeah, it's awesome. Looks great, sounds epic, types even better.

Alright, so this one isn't actually a mechanical board. It's magnetic. However, the K2 HE is still an absolute weapon for typing — adjustable actuation lets you dial in your switch behavior to optimize type speeds. And naturally, as a Hall Effect deck, it's a total demon for gaming too.

I tested the NuPhy Air75 V3, this board's little sibling, and absolutely loved it. If you're after a low-profile board with drop-dead gorgeous looks, captivating sound and effortless typing, here it is.

Still probably the best sounding keyboard we've ever tested, I spent several weeks using the Rainy 75 Pro as my daily driver at work. The creamy raindrop-esque clack is utterly addictive, and this board is a perfect candidate for modding too.

Arguably rather overpriced at MSRP, the Lofree DOT still captured my heart when I reviewed it. Lofree's styling is second to none, and the DOT's circular keycaps give you that retro type-writer-esque experience. It's still expensive at this sale price, but a hell of a lot more palatable than the list price, and I'd definitely say worth it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, EXCLUSIVE: Greg Hovanessian (The Mist, Cardinal) and Lindsey Normington (Margo’s Got Money Troubles, Anora) are set to lead the new psychological thriller Nightwaves, from writer and director Kristian McKay (Do Not Open, Kill Trip) and Obscura Film. Cherie Currie (Foxes, Twilight Zone: The Movie) and Shane Coffey (Pretty Little Liars, Good Girls) will also star.

It has been revealed that set against the dark, desolate highways of Texas, Nightwaves unfolds over the course of a single night, following Mason (Hovanessian), a young man driving alone whose unexpected phone conversation with a mysterious woman (Normington) offers an initially welcome escape. As their exchange shifts from flirtation to increasingly unsettling questions, the woman on the other end of the line begins to threaten everything Mason is desperately trying to leave behind. With each passing mile, he finds himself moving closer to a confrontation he cannot simply hang up to avoid. Related Stories Casting Jillian Moray Sets Directorial Debut 'Pismo,' Stars Opposite Nuha Jes Izman, Madeline Popovich & More News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Heading To Potential Franchise-Record Monday With $12M.

Currie and Coffey’s roles are under wraps. Watch on Deadline.

Production is presently underway in San Antonio and the surrounding Texas landscape.

In a recent development, “There’s something incredibly intimate about talking to someone in the dark when you can’t see their face. You start filling in the blanks, and that can be seductive or terrifying,” shared McKay. “With Nightwaves, I want the audience to feel that connection tightening until it becomes a trap. Greg and Lindsey bring the vulnerability and unpredictability these roles demand, and having Cherie and Shane in this world gives the film such a distinct personality.”.

According to recent reports, obscura Film touts in a release how “McKay will bring a distinctive visual approach to the thriller, allowing tension and performances to unfold in extended, uninterrupted moments. Using the empty stretches of highway, passing headlights, and the confined interior of a moving car, the film transforms an ordinary phone conversation into an increasingly claustrophobic psychological experience, where what remains unseen may be more terrifying than anything in view.”.

According to recent reports, the film is produced by Obscura Film partners Daunesh Alcott and McKay, alongside Jose Corres. Executive produced by Gustavo Oliveira.

Recent findings suggest that nightwaves expands Obscura Film’s growing slate of independently produced genre features. The project follows Kill Trip, acquired by Quiver Distribution and released in 2026, and Do Not Open, McKay’s supernatural thriller starring Freddy Carter, Lulu Wilson, Mark McKenna, John Ford Coley and Stelio Savante, which is right now in post-production.

According to recent reports, hovanessian is repped by Robert Stein Management and Clear Talent Group. Normington is repped by Innovative Artists and Authentic Talent & Literary Management. Coffey is repped by Industry Entertainment and Pakula/ King.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

The case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

If you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

Recent findings suggest that I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $149. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

It has been revealed that finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

According to recent reports, this year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

AirPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

In a recent development, if you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

It has been revealed that are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

#154184. Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bertptrs

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself.
  • In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.
  • Industry observers note that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.

Industry observers note that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:.

The following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError), which will trigger a panic when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

Industry observers note that you might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this is the common case.

In a recent development, I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she works on lend themselves more towards these issues compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t ready to kill my darlings.1 Skip to the next section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

In a recent development, in Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex2 system call. It allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three unique values:.

Flow chart showing how a mutex acquisition is implemented in Rust, using atomic operations and futex primitives. Note how the uncontended case remains entirely in user-space and does not sleep the thread.

Rust implements this with a few atomic operations and the futex_wait call. Crucially, the path for locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that requires a context switch is futex_wait.

Unlocking is even simpler. The thread that holds the mutex first releases the lock, then optionally, if there was an indication that the lock was contended, wakes any sleeping threads so they can try to acquire the lock.

Flow chart showing how a mutex release in Rust. First, we swap the current value with 0, and depending on whether it was originally 1 (simply locked) or 2 (contended), we optionally wake any sleeping threads.

Sources indicate that as discussed in too much detail above, (un)locking mutexes is cheap as long as they’re not contended, and when contended, they are at least cheap instruction wise. This is where poisoning mutexes get you.

Recent findings suggest that in short, being able to poison is a cost that is always paid, but seldom used. To start, poisoning is essentially implemented by adding an AtomicBool field to every Mutex. Due to alignment, this grows the size of every mutex by anywhere from zero bytes to an additional pointer. This isn’t terrible but for use cases where you have many mutexes guarding small objects, this can add up.

In a recent development, the real issue to me however is in code size. Let’s start with another contrived example, a function that reads its argument, copies it, and returns it. An idealised version of that would be the following.

This compiles down to 2 instructions and a label. Copy the data into the register then return.

Of course, this doesn’t work for any context that needs shared mutation, but we can consider it our baseline. Perfection would look like this. So, let’s ignore that atomic integers exist and add a mutex to this story. We will go over the generated assembly code for each, and you can compare the code in its entirety in this Compiler Explorer overview.

We can upgrade the code above to actually use mutexes, and simply lock-then-unwrap the mutex.

This compiles to a total of 147 lines of assembly which I’m not going to reproduce here in full.

To divide that up a different way, we have.

Most of this is inlined into the function. This in turn affects performance, as this limits how much of your “real” code fits in the CPU’s instruction cache. The laptop I’m writing this on has a paltry 32KiB of instruction cache. Luckily we can do better.

Most of the code generated in the previous example had to do with setting up the panic, and checking the conditions. But we don’t care about panicking. We can simply acknowledge the PoisonError and continue. That looks as follows:.

It has been revealed that this results in only 68 lines of assembly, which is much better, though all of it is inlined to our function. Compared to before, we’ve lost all panic related code. There’s still some unnecessary branching related to whether the mutex is poisoned, as well as a little dance to track poisoning in our function. Our function can never panic, but compiler optimisations currently do not remove the atomic loads and stores involved here. Nevertheless, if you want to target stable Rust and you don’t care about panics, this is what you should do at the moment.

In the current nightly builds of Rust, there are non-poisoning mutexes that can don’t have any of the overhead. We can optimise our code from above to make use of them.

Recent findings suggest that no unwrapping, and it only results in 34 lines of assembly code. This is short enough for me to walk through it.

Industry observers note that I’ve added comments and labels to the assembly so the steps from the (un)locking flow charts become visible. As far as assembly code goes, it’s very readable and simple. Which, of course, is exactly what you want from fundamental library code.

The additional logic checking the poison state, adding a destructor for the mutex guard, and, if you choose ergonomics, even panic machinery, significantly bloats the code of a rather fundamental operation.

According to recent reports, besides the purely technical argument that poisoning makes all code larger and slower than it needs to be, there is a different one. As discussed previously, code that doesn’t care about mutex poisoning should generally write:.

It’s reasonably efficient and available on stable Rust. But that whole unwrap_or_else part takes up more than half the line. No worry, you might say, we can make it shorter:.

This works well enough. It’s less efficient than the previous example, but it’s nice and short. If your code never panics, it’s even perfectly safe. You might have spotted a load-bearing “if” already. It’s kind of hard to guarantee your code does not panic. Array indexing, integer division, and a whole host of other features might panic unexpectedly.

Sources indicate that this is hard for experienced developers, but for those learning it’s even worse. It also trains bad habits. Every time a beginner Rust developer writes unwrap() instead of handling their errors, a puppy steps on a Lego brick. Or causes a widespread internet outage. One of the two, I forget which.

We should not want to include APIs into the standard library that return a Result that is “expected” to be unwrapped. Infallible operations should not fail.

Poisoning protects against a task panicking in the middle of an invariant violation. But why must this be specific to mutexes? The example from before works just as well with a simple mutable borrow. Panics may still happen, and you may still catch them.

In a recent development, this is actually a fairly common problem. In a more recent blog post, researchers at Microsoft highlight various places they’ve found where even the standard library gets this wrong.

In most cases however, this is fine, as it is with the mutex example given in the beginning. You don’t need to poison this reference. But for applications where you do, it’s kinda nice to be able to.

It’s not hard to imagine a wrapper that adds poisoning behaviour when you want to have it. Crucially, this needs to be an additive wrapper. You can add a poisoning system to something. You cannot strip out the poisoning system from a primitive that has it. Poison safety is important for the specific use cases that need it, but most do not.

I don’t believe it’s worth it to saddle mutexes in particular with this overhead when the problem is near universal with any mutable state. State invariants are just hard that way.

Sources indicate that one might draw a comparison between poison safety and buffer safety. In Rust, we always do bounds checking, relying on the compiler to optimise it out in cases it can be proven redundant. Can’t poison safety be the same? And the answer, it turns out, is no.

According to recent reports, the compiler cannot optimise poisoning away. It requires any mutex carry additional data to track it. Maybe the compiler can figure out one particular critical section cannot panic, and therefore it can leave out the setup and clean-up, but in general it cannot avoid checking the state. This is overhead that always applies, and hurts, especially in environments where code size is more restricted.

Recent findings suggest that in C++, there are a few choices in the standard that make certain containers less efficient than they could be4. Because of how standardisation works, the containers can never be “fixed”. This causes third party implementations, such as Abseil and Boost, to become the de facto standard.

Mutexes in Rust suffer from the same problem. The standard library has poisoning, but people don’t want poisoning, so instead they opt for crates like parking_lot. I believe this is bad for the ecosystem as a whole. When the standard library offers a feature, it should be an uncontroversially good choice, unless you are doing something hyper specific. We don’t have to be “batteries included” but the parts that are there should be a good fit.

It has been revealed that rain’s blog argued for option 1. I believe we both agree that option 2 is a terrible idea. I think we should do at least option 3. Option 4 would be a good edition improvement, but it is also a significant compatibility problem, and even I find it hard to argue that it’s really worth it.

Which is a roundabout way of saying that we really should stabilise std::sync::nonpoison and definitely should not make std::sync::Mutex panic by default.

It is becoming apparent to me that I just like explaining mutexes and I don’t know what to do about that. ↩︎.

Fast Userspace muTEX. See futex(2) for more on the system call and futex(7) for its semantics ↩︎.

It has been revealed that for generic definitions (e.g. Mutex) the compiler must generate code for every unique T that gets used, and for loads of reasons often more than once per T. The compiler development docs have a deeper explanation of monomorphisation. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, A famous example is std::unordered_map, which suffers from being over-specified and that prevents more efficient implementations. ↩︎.
