#154146. Nospeaker ─ Make your MacBook's trackpad talk using its haptic motor

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Nospeaker ─ Make your MacBook's trackpad talk using its haptic motor

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there's no speaker in a MacBook trackpad, just a small haptic motor that taps the glass so you feel a click.
  • Downloads the latest release to ~/.local/bin/nospeaker and starts the show.
  • Industry observers note that grab nospeaker.zip from the latest release, unzip it and run ./nospeaker in Terminal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mute your Mac. Your trackpad will still talk.

According to recent reports, there's no speaker in a MacBook trackpad, just a small haptic motor that taps the glass so you feel a click. NO SPEAKER drives that motor up to 4,000 times a second, fast enough to make sound you can hear, and turns it into a voice. It talks, sings, raps, and becomes an instrument under your finger.

One command. About a minute and a half. No speakers used.

Space skips a part. q or Ctrl-C goes to the end.

Downloads the latest release to ~/.local/bin/nospeaker and starts the show. a90.com/nospeaker points to play.sh in this repo, so you can read what it runs first.

Industry observers note that grab nospeaker.zip from the latest release, unzip it and run ./nospeaker in Terminal. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

Needs Xcode or the Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install). Builds one program for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

Sources indicate that A Force Touch trackpad (built into MacBooks from 2015 on, or a Magic Trackpad 2 or newer), and macOS 12 or later on Apple Silicon, or macOS 13 or later on Intel. Without a Force Touch trackpad, it says so and exits.

Not tested yet: Intel Macs, a Magic Trackpad, and older versions of macOS. MultitouchSupport is private, so older systems may lack the functions it uses, and loudness differs between trackpads. If you try it on another Mac, open an concern with your model, your macOS version and how it sounded.

Why you can hear it. The trackpad has no speaker, but the motor moves the glass. Driven back and forth hundreds or thousands of times a second, the glass vibrates fast enough to make sound you can hear. It's quiet because the motor is built for short taps, not for sound.

Industry observers note that the motor. MultitouchSupport is the private framework macOS uses for the trackpad. Its function MTActuationCreateFromDictionary takes a description of a vibration, a list of sine tones with a frequency, a strength and a length each, and MTActuationActuate plays it on the motor. Apple's public haptics API only offers three fixed taps.

It has been revealed that the range. Measured with the MacBook's own microphone, every semitone from 98 Hz to 3,951 Hz: how loud it is over a quiet room, and how much of the sound is the note itself.

It's loud from about 100 Hz to 4 kHz, with a few dead spots where the glass resonates. Its loudest, cleanest notes are around 1 kHz, which covers the most important part of a voice.

Industry observers note that the voice. macOS's own voice speaks the line into memory. Every 10 ms, linear prediction finds the voice's two strongest resonances (formants), its loudness and its pitch. The motor plays those two resonances as tones, restarted on every beat of the pitch, so they buzz like a voice instead of whistling. Hiss sounds (s, f, t) become quick bursts of high tones. Two resonances beat three: in a blind test they were clearer, and louder, because the motor's strength is split fewer ways.

It sounds robotic, and it's much easier to follow when you can read along, which is why the show types every line as it speaks.

It has been revealed that the code. One Swift file, nospeaker.swift, with no dependencies.

The MultitouchSupport function names were learned from the open-source Tactile project. Everything else was measured on a MacBook.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Effective immediately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors just voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as President, CEO and board director — just 11 days after he resigned amid an explosive espionage and extramarital affair scandal, and a mere six days after the company insisted it had no intention of bringing him back.

If you blinked over the last two weeks, you might have missed the entire post-Jensen Huang era of Nvidia. It is the kind of corporate whiplash that makes Sam Altman’s infamous five-day OpenAI ousting look like PTO. To make sense of how the world’s most consequential chipmaker pulled off a full-speed reverse, you have to look at the sheer chaos of the last 25 days.

So what changed between last Tuesday’s firm “no” and this morning’s unanimous “welcome back”?

Sources indicate that according to Nvidia’s official announcement, two things broke the deadlock: a series of sitdowns where the board became “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead,” and — crucially — a green light from Washington.

The board explicitly noted that it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Combine that quiet federal clearance with an internal employee revolt, vocal backing from the White House and a brutal month on the stock ticker, and the board’s math became pretty simple.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones remarked in Monday’s statement, thanking Colette Kress for holding the fort as interim CEO before returning to her full-time CFO duties.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Huang, for his part, struck a notably humbler tone than the usual keynote bravado I’ve seen in person a few times.

"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment... Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work." — Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO.

Industry observers note that before you get too excited with “WE ARE SO BACK” responses and “stonks” GIFs, read the fine print at the bottom of Nvidia’s press release. Huang may have his title back, but he’s walking back into a very different corporate structure — and the legal storm hasn’t magically evaporated:.

If you were hoping that two weeks of boardroom chaos at Nvidia would pop the AI bubble and magically bring back $90 DDR5 kits (like me), I have some bad news: Jensen Huang’s comeback just put the AI infrastructure train right back at full throttle.

With Wall Street cheering his return and Washington clearing the runway, hyperscalers aren’t tapping the brakes on data center spending anytime soon.

That means Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron have zero reason to pull wafers off high-margin data center memory and send them back to everyday PC builders — especially with Trendforce expecting DRAM prices to climb another 10-15% this quarter and stay tight well into 2027.

Does that mean the dream of RAMageddon dying is gone? Not quite — it just changes your game plan.

Industry observers note that if you see a legitimate Black Friday deal that actually undercuts pre-crisis pricing, treat it like an escape hatch. Waiting for “cheaper RAM next spring” is a gamble that’s looking worse by the hour.

According to recent reports, there is one genuine silver lining. While DRAM stays squeezed, Trendforce’s latest forecast shows NAND flash prices finally turning the corner and starting to dip as early as Q1 2027 — so unless you spot a genuinely fair Black Friday deal, don’t let retailers gouge you on storage right now.

Nvidia’s rebound might keep AI demand humming, but it doesn’t bail the memory giants out of their California antitrust lawsuit or stop the mainstream backlash over inflated PC prices.

Recent findings suggest that jensen getting his desk back is great news for Nvidia shareholders. For the rest of us just trying to buy a computer without paying an absurd memory tax, the message is simple: grab the real Black Friday bargains while they exist, ignore the fake red discount stickers, and buckle in — RAMageddon isn’t packing its bags just yet.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

Industry observers note that I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Hopefully backlit keyboard if they increase price.

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the company also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

If there is a price increase, it likely won’t be too major, maybe $50 – leaving the computer at $749. Compared to the rest of the laptop landscape, MacBook Neo would still be a good value. We’ll see what happens.

Apple's fresh releases are among the products we don't often see on sale, even around Black Friday. After all, they usually sell well, so there's no reason for Apple to drop the price.

Sources indicate that but that's exactly what's happening with the newly introduced iPad mini. It's $100 off as part of Amazon's early Black Friday deals, which is a tremendous deal on a product our own Jason England noted is worth canceling your iPhone Duo pre-order for, as long as you pair it with a traditional iPhone.

This is Apple's best small iPad ever, and the only real complaint about it was the price; with $100 off, that issue is completely negated.

In a recent development, the iPad mini just got a massive refresh. It has a larger 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR Display (2316 x 1512), an A20 Pro CPU (a powerhouse), 24% smaller bezels than its predecessor, and better audio. So even with the bigger screen, it's still a super-compact device. It has a 12MP camera on the front and back with full Wi-Fi 7 support for fast connectivity.

Sources indicate that if you're curious what makes the latest iPad mini worth buying, it really comes down to performance. The new A20 Chip is shockingly good at handling anything you could ever want to throw at it.

It's so good, in fact, that our lab tester Arif Bacchus ditched the ultra-expensive 12-inch iPad Pro M1 in favor of the svelte 8.5-inch iPad mini. It sounds like a crazy decision, but it makes a lot more sense than it might appear when you consider how capable this tiny device actually is.

"As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip. Paired with a solid trade-in offer for my older Pro, I couldn’t resist the urge to get one for myself," wrote Bacchus.

In a recent development, our reviewer, Tony Polanco, gave Apple's latest small tablet a 4.5-star rating, citing the thinner design, vibrant OLED panel, fast A20 Pro performance, epic battery life, and rich speaker sound as the reasons for the high score. The only negative aspects of the device are the lack of Face ID and the limited screen refresh rate, but those are fairly minor compared with all the positives.

At the end of the day, the iPad mini is the world's best small tablet, and now it's the easily one of the best iPad deals for Black Friday.

Management shares three key insights on how the organization plans to navigate this environment.

Systems and Services revenue dropped 7.6% year over year as practices shifted toward leasing, rentals, and lower-priced hardware options. Management expects these flexible arrangements to lower adoption hurdles, expand the installed base, and drive recurring software revenue over time.

The company is applying its direct fabrication technology from orthodontic appliances like palatal expanders into new product lines, starting with custom sports mouthguards. Management aims to leverage this direct fabrication platform to increase brand awareness among younger patients and raise doctor utilization rates.

Sources indicate that manufacturing automation, higher factory productivity, and lower treatment refinement rates lifted non-GAAP operating margin, an adjusted measure that excludes one-time charges, to 24.4%. Financial planning for 2027 relies on internal expense discipline rather than assuming a recovery in discretionary consumer spending.

Industry observers note that soft consumer demand continues to pressure discretionary healthcare spending, but operational execution creates clear pathways to growth across global markets. Expanding digital workflows, deeper relationships with dental service organizations, and proprietary direct fabrication offer structural advantages as hardware pricing stabilizes. Management monitors doctor utilization rates, patient financing adoption, and operating discipline to protect profitability.

Automation efforts and strategic cost reviews support ongoing operational expansion. Management targets steady efficiency gains while funding core digital platforms and returning capital through share repurchases.

These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers.
  • According to recent reports, because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives.
  • The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

According to recent reports, because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the organization introduced a upcoming model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

Industry observers note that if you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is at the moment $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

Sources indicate that the new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's at the moment pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, at the moment marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (presently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Industry observers note that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

It has been revealed that no. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

We will keep adding fresh capabilities â hereâs what to expect over the next few quarters.

Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.

Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. Youâll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone.

AI copycats are cloning creators’ videos for millions of views, BBC finds

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Musicians, dancers and comedians are finding their videos copied by AI-generated characters, BBC Verify reported.
  • Experts call the practice “reskinning”.
  • Industry observers note that UK guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with Machine Gun Kelly, indicates accounts keep reskinning her performances with over-sexualised AI characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Musicians, dancers and comedians are finding their videos copied by AI-generated characters, BBC Verify reported. The copies repeat the same performance, sometimes to millions more viewers. Marco Silva found accounts that copy a real person’s clip frame by frame and swap the person for an AI character.

Experts call the practice “reskinning”. Cheap AI tools make it easy: the copy keeps the same joke, the same dance and often the same background. Some accounts use it for views and money, the BBC found. Others seem to do it for laughs or attention.

Industry observers note that UK guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with Machine Gun Kelly, indicates accounts keep reskinning her performances with over-sexualised AI characters. One Facebook account posted hundreds of videos of a guitarist called “Mila Vasari”. At least three copied Lloyd’s music, movements and facial expressions, BBC Verify found.

Sources indicate that the BBC found no evidence that Vasari is real. Her fingers look distorted and the strings don’t move. The account appears to be run from Canada. It links to a Vasari page on Fanvue, a subscription site that allows adult content. It did not answer the BBC’s questions. Two more accounts with AI guitarists copied Lloyd to promote adult content.

“It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else,” Lloyd told the BBC.

Norwegian creator Kjetil Krogstad, known for dancing in a suit with a cup of tea, saw one video redone with an AI bunny. The copy drew millions more views than his original before it disappeared. The account behind it sold courses on making money from AI content.

According to recent reports, british car creator Grace Roberts found her video remade with a blonde woman in a short dress. The copy kept her movements, the background and even the people around her.

“It was just me that had been altered,” Roberts told BBC Verify.

Sources indicate that many copies follow videos that are already popular, mentioned Tina Kendall, who studies online culture at Anglia Ruskin University. She described the copies as part of an online “hustle culture”. Alwyn Cruz, who exposes AI musicians online, said new accounts appear as soon as platforms remove old ones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after reviewing close to 100 coffee makers in the last 5 years, we've yet to find a machine that can beat the formidable Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV Select. Durable, consistent and iconic for a reason, it's back at the top of our guide after we re-reviewed it in early 2026.

But while we think the Moccamaster is the best coffee maker for most people, there are so many types and brands of coffee maker to choose from. If you're looking for a great espresso machine, it's the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch we recommend above all others. Its compact design and advanced features combine customisable elements with a user-assisted interface that will make it easy to craft delectable espresso.

I've been reviewing coffee makers for over six years, and I never log on for a day of work without two shots of espresso in my system. An SCA-certified barista, I've tested everything from a $9 French press to a $3,000 espresso machine. I'd happily drink a brew made in any of the seven machines I've featured in my carefully-curated list of the best coffee makers. So if you want an expert-approved brewer, just keep scrolling.

Recent findings suggest that it's late November, which means Black Friday deals are live. Our on-page tech in this guide will show you when there are discounts on our favorite machines, but if you're looking for more coffee deals over the holiday season, we're continually updating our roundup of the best Black Friday deals, including coffee makers like the Keurig K-Express which is almost half price right now. Or, if you're after inspiration for the enthusiast in your life, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers this holiday season.

In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Sources indicate that we've reviewed nearly a dozen coffee makers so far this year, and most notably, reviewer Erin re-tested the iconic Moccamaster, which we last put through its paces back in 2021. We wanted to see if it still held its own against the many outstanding releases of the last few years. And the answer is a resounding yes. Now back at the top of our guide, it's certainly the one to beat for the rest of the year's top releases.

Compiling this buying guide has required a lot of evaluation and comparison between completely unrelated methods of brewing, as well as machines that span from $50 to well over $2,000. How, you might wonder, can we rank these machines if they're being tested against completely different criteria?

It's true, I'd never tell you to buy a drip coffee maker if you love espresso, and we'd never tell you to buy the most premium machine if you're on a budget, so before you buy, you need to have a rough idea of what kind of coffee you actually want to make at home.

Recent findings suggest that in this guide, I've included drip coffee makers, as well as a range of single-serve machines and espresso machines. And when ranking these products, I've considered what's right for most people. I know a lot more about coffee than the majority of buyers, so I had to go back to basics when writing this guide to make it accessible to everyone.

It has been revealed that even within the Tom's Guide team, there's a huge range of coffee preferences. There are some people who would turn their nose up at a cup of pod coffee, and would never consider straying from their carefully evaluated coffee setup.

For others, coffee is simply a tool for waking up in the morning, and you just want a reliable and space-efficient gadget to fill your cup with something cheaper and better than the stuff you'd get from a chain coffee shop. That's ok too, because you know your budget, and you know what you're looking for. And no matter what it is that you're seeking, I'm confident that I've included it in this guide.

Each and every machine has been hand-selected and tested by myself or one of Tom's Guide's expert testers, so you can click through to read full, detailed reviews before you make up your mind.

The Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV Select has been in this buying guide for five years, but a lot has changed since our first review in 2021. So in early 2026, we took it for another spin to see if it can hold its own against the latest and greatest releases.

Sources indicate that well, the results are in, and the Moccamaster is still the cream of the crop. Hand-made in the Netherlands, the brand has a well-deserved reputation for quality construction and dependable results. It's not the cheapest option, but if you treat it with care, it will last a lifetime.

Reviewer Erin noted "the Moccamaster is so famous because nothing really compares. Nothing comes close. The Moccamaster has been topping “best-of” lists before best-of lists were even a thing — it’s reigned supreme since the ‘60s.".

It has been revealed that compared to feature-rich options like the Ratio Four, Breville Luxe Brewer, or OXO Brew 8-Cup, the Moccamaster stands out for its simplicity and efficiency. It forgoes extras like cold brew modes or app controls, but it’s faster than the Ratio Four, easier to use than the Breville Luxe Brewer, and delivers a more consistent cup than the OXO. The machine offers simplicity and ease of use in everyday drip brewing.

Industry observers note that to use, simply add your water to the tank and your grounds to the filter, and switch it on. However, it's this simplicity that has earned special recognition from the Specialty Coffee Association. Using a copper heating element and precise brew temperature control, the KBGV Select can hit industry-standard temperatures between 196°F and 205°F in under a minute and, crucially, stay there throughout the entire brewing process. The gentle showerhead-style water dispenser will evenly agitate coffee grounds to create a balanced extraction.

Industry observers note that the Breville Bambino Plus has been on the market for seven years, but it's still one of the most popular espresso machines ever released. If you're based in Europe (like me) you'll know this brand as Sage, but the machines are otherwise the same.

With groundbreaking automatic steaming technology, which is still top of the line nearly a decade later, this is the espresso machine for you if you're in the market for an entry-level machine with some serious power.

Sources indicate that we made some outstanding shots of espresso with this gadget. I'm talking drool-worthy toffee-colored strands of crema and a vibrant extraction that tasted fantastic. You should note, this machine doesn't have a grinder built in.

You'll want to pair it with one of the best coffee grinders (you can buy a good one for around $100, and our reviews walk you through all the options) for the ideal espresso, but if you use a double-walled portafilter you can still achieve a lively brew when using pre-ground coffee.

As for the automatic milk steaming, this thing can achieve a very fine micro-foam that's totally latte art-worthy, completely hands-free. And it automatically purges after each use, which will keep the steam wand clog-free and running smoothly (so long as you descale regularly).

Sources indicate that if you want a single-serve coffee maker that can truly do it all, you should look no further than the Nespresso Vertuo Lattissima. Featuring a separate milk dispenser that offers milk-only drinks and two lengths of milk add-ins to any coffee size you opt for, the beauty of this machine is in its simplicity.

You can simply store the milk dispenser in the refrigerator when it's not in use, and you'll get the joys of the entirety of Nespresso's six-size Vertuo system if you prefer a long black coffee or an espresso to start the day.

Recent findings suggest that we enjoyed the thoughtful touches such as an adjustable cup holder to work with any beverage size, and the ability to rinse out the milk dispenser after each use. We did wish that there were more than one milk froth level available, because if you prefer a firmer layer to make an espresso or a softer latte-style steamed milk, you won't be able to adjust this using the Nespresso.

Because this machine is part of the Vertuo line it will automatically brew the optimum drink length for each drink and you can enjoy an ever-evolving list of capsules to mix up your routine. We even tried a cold-brew capsule, which was impressively realistic.

Sometimes, simple is better. The OXO Brew 8-Cup is one such machine. It's shy on buttons and limited on features, but this machine undeniably makes tasty coffee, and it's SCA-certified to prove it.

You can brew either 2-4 cups or 5-8 cups with the OXO Brew. It simply requires you to fill up the water tank to your desired cup amount, load up a filter and coffee grounds, then hit start.

According to recent reports, there's beauty in the simplicity, though. Its rainshower distribution ensures that grounds are soaked evenly and consistently before extraction, meaning you won't be left with anemic or muddy coffee, and your coffee will never taste burnt from uncontrolled water temperatures.

Another plus is the double-walled carafe. This will keep your brew hot for a couple of hours, making it ideal for busy households. Reviewer Camryn's only complaint was the water tank, which can't be removed. That's annoying, but it's nothing a jug can't fix.

Somehow, the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch manages to be both super-smart and aesthetically pleasing, while also compact enough for small kitchens. It's no mean feat, and one that won the machine the top spot in our best espresso machine buying guide.

The main addition is the responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen, which walks you through everything from dialing in your beans (finding the right grind size for your specific brew) to automatically steaming the milk for the drink of your choosing.

Industry observers note that while there are plenty of excellent automatic features here, this machine also lets you take the reins, which will be a welcome feature for those who want to work on their home barista skills. I enjoyed hand-steaming with this machine, and was able to toggle with finer features to really master every espresso.

It's a small feature, but De'Longhi should take a bow for how compact the La Specialista Touch is. It slotted easily onto my countertops, which often look drowned by larger coffee makers. And despite its compact size, it still does literally everything you could want from an espresso machine.

While it looks like a drip coffee maker, the Ratio Four is actually an automated pour-over coffee maker. So if you love pour-over, but don't love the laborious process of brewing it, the Ratio Four is for you.

With a sleek, minimalist appearance and straightforward operation, the Ratio took just under seven minutes to brew a 20-ounce serving of coffee, and one cup was complete in three and a half minutes.

Reviewer Erin recommends this option for serious coffee lovers. She called it "sophisticated enough to excite even the most fastidious coffee shop hipster," noting that "if you’re familiar with coffee bean varieties and the phrases “pre-infusion” and “optimal flow rate” don’t scare you off, this is the machine for you.".

Recent findings suggest that the main downside of this brewer is its lack of 'keep warm' setting. Unlike your average drip brewer, it's not designed with bulk brewing in mind. This one's for the true coffee enthusiasts, who would never dream of reheating a precious V60 brew. If you do want a keep-warm option, check out the Moccamaster or Breville Luxe.

The Terra Kaffe Demi is a standout choice for those who want café-quality drinks at home with zero fuss. Its intuitive interface and one-touch operation make espresso simple, so you can enjoy impressive coffee without mastering barista skills or fiddling with settings.

There are downsides to superautomatic espresso machines, which is why few have scored highly in our rigorous Barista-led testing. But where the locked-away grinding, brewing and steaming mechanisms may feel restrictive for coffee enthusiasts, if your key concern is reliability and ease of use, you can't go wrong with the likes of the Terra Kaffe.

Industry observers note that machines that require manual tamping or careful monitoring, such as the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, can't match the Demi's ease of use. Simply press a button, add your beans, and it will craft anything from a piping hot espresso to a long black Americano in minutes. There's one major con: it doesn't have a milk frother, which many superautomatic machines from the likes of Jura and De'Longhi do offer.

For anyone who wants the easiest possible coffee routine, the Demi’s accessible cleaning features are a relief. After a month of daily use, review Dan found maintenance practically painless. Pop out the brew group for a rinse, and you’re done. If you want hands-off, great-tasting espresso with minimal upkeep, the Demi delivers. But if you're a coffee lover who knows their arabica from their robusta, its lack of customisation may prove frustrating.

I joined Tom's Guide in 2024 on the product reviews team. While I test everything from keyboards to vacuum cleaners, I'm also a former barista with years and years of experience, which is why I'm Tom's Guide's go-to coffee maker tester.

I've tested a number of leading espresso machines from Smeg and KitchenAid, as well as other brewing methods such as the AeroPress. I've also been down to Smeg and La Pavoni HQ to get hands-on with some high-tech gear.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

Sources indicate that as a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, coffee machines.

At the end of the day, the most important sign of a good coffee maker comes down to that all-important taste test. So it goes without saying that I taste a lot of coffee when putting together my coffee maker reviews. However, there are endless factors that can determine the flavor of your finished coffee, so there are some metrics I need to consider (and keep consistent) when testing coffee makers and curating buying guides.

In a recent development, the most sustainable choice you can make when buying a new coffee maker is opting for a machine that will last for years and years. That stated, it's a good sign when a coffee maker comes in recyclable, sustainable packaging that still keeps it secure during shipping, so I'm always looking out for this when evaluating my first impressions of a product.

In my experience, a more drawn-out setup process can be worth the extra hassle. Some coffee makers have a water hardness strip included to input the limescale level in your water. This test takes a few extra minutes, but inputting this information will ensure the machine reminds you to descale it as and when needed to prolong its lifespan.

If a coffee maker comes with an app or any bespoke programming such as personalized profiles or pre-set timers, we troubleshoot this in testing to make sure you're getting an easy-to-use machine from the very first use.

According to recent reports, coffee makers don't have to be expensive — especially if you're buying a single-serve or drip coffee maker, but it's often the case that you get what you pay for with coffee makers. When testing I evaluate if this is the case. Does a $1,000+ coffee maker really warrant the price tag, and most importantly, would I recommend it to a friend or family member who was shopping for a new machine?

Your cup of coffee can only be as good as the grounds you use, so when testing, I try and opt for an accessible consumer blend and stick to this brand across models to ensure that the differences we taste in our coffee come from the quality of the machine, and not the beans.

As a basic rule, I use fresh-roasted arabica beans in every review. This allows the taste and extraction of every coffee to shine through. And while I don't expect that every home tester will be splashing out on artisan beans, at least this way you know you're getting a machine that can create some seriously tasty coffee if you ever decide to level up from those kilo bags of robusta.

It has been revealed that this is particularly important for drip coffee makers. I test the temperature of each carafe I make when it's first brewed, and then after one hour, to test the quality of the heating plate on each machine.

It has been revealed that if freshly brewed coffee comes out too hot, it's a sign that the machine has scorched the grounds in testing, which will result in a more bitter flavor and is a sign of a poorly-made machine. Likewise, if the coffee is not hot enough, you won't get a fully developed flavor and your coffee will be weak and acidic.

Industry observers note that some coffee makers come with in-built grinders, so I put them through a similar process to our standalone reviews for the best coffee grinders. This involves testing the variety of grind sizes available, and how suitable this is for the type of coffee maker you're using. If your espresso maker's grinder creates great grounds for filter coffee, that's not much help!

I use a coffee sifter called Kruve to see how consistent the coffee grounds are in size and texture, and we also test coffee grinders for static.

If an espresso machine comes with a hand milk steamer, there is an inevitable margin for user error when testing. Fortunately, I have a team of expert testers on-hand who have steamed more than a few lattes in their time, so if they find fault with a steamer, I can confidently say it's a flaw in design.

When steaming milk, I look for a smooth and fine micro-foam that doesn't burn the milk before we're able to get the consistency we want.

Some machines come with automatic frothers, and while it's hard for these to recreate a hand-steaming effect, I look for how easy they are to use and how close they come to the real thing.

If all of this seems a bit overwhelming, we've tried to simplify the category a bit and help you decide on which type of coffee maker you should buy.

We test a lot of coffee makers. It feels like there's always a upcoming innovation to put through its paces, so our testing team can be found reliably caffeinated on any given day.

We return most of the coffee makers we test due to the high value of these machines, but on the occasion that we're allowed to keep one, we continue to test them from home in order to evaluate the value for money over time, and compare our old faithfuls to recent releases.

In a recent development, not every coffee maker can make the list though. Here are some of the models we've recently tried.

The xBloom is one of the most interesting drip coffee makers on the market, with legions of fans who love getting involved with every step of the brewing process.

Read the full xBloom Drip Coffee Maker review.

Gevi 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker (★★☆☆☆).

Let's just say Erin did not enjoy the Gevi. Its in-built grinder is really, really bad, which means it's impossible to get a decent brew out of this machine.

Read the full Gevi 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker review.

Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

Smeg teamed up with La Pavoni, makers of the original espresso machine, to create the EMC02. And it lives up to the hype. In testing, Erin found that it's the closest she's got to professional equipment at home.

Read the full Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine review.

Erin described the De'Longhi Rivelia as a coffee-making robot. This superautomatic does it all, from grinding your beans to order to frothing just the right amount of milk for your desired drink. Its smart interface is what sets it apart, with different user profiles allowing you to interact with the machine depending on everything from your go-to drink to the time of day. We couldn't add it to the guide because, while it's very well-priced in the U.K., the price in America is a bit exorbitant for what you get.

Cheap and plasticky the Stilosa may be, but we found that it's capable of making a mean cup of coffee. We don't recommend it for beginners, but if you're on a budget and are willing to put in the hours, it's a good option.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop Plus (★★★★☆).

There's only so good Nespresso coffee can taste, so you may as well get one of the brand's cheaper machines, especially if you're not concerned with milk-based drinks. The Pop+ is compact and cute to look at, but it drips a lot and won't fit every mug. If you're looking for a neat little machine, it's a savvy option — especially if you find it on sale.

Recent findings suggest that amazon-favorite brand Casabrews offers suspiciously affordable espresso machines which certainly look the part, but can they deliver? Surprisingly, they kind of can. Breville Oracle Dual Boiler (★★★★☆).

It has been revealed that the Oracle Dual Boiler is Breville's latest, and dare we say, greatest release. It's massively expensive: $3,000, which makes it a tough machine to recommend. This superpowered brewer offers pro-level specs, but reviewer Pete didn't love the grinder.

Read the full Breville Oracle Dual Boiler review.

Keurig K-Duo Hot & Iced (★★★★☆).

Sources indicate that there’s nothing like a great cup of coffee to wake you up in the morning, so if you’re looking to invest in a upcoming coffee maker, you’ll want one that makes the ideal brew, provides the functionality and practicality you desire and comes in on budget. Here are a few things you’ll need to think about.

Will it fit?A coffee maker sits on the countertop, so measure the space where you blueprint to keep the machine before you buy one. Be sure to determine the clearance between the countertop and the bottom of your cabinets. Most, but not all coffee makers will fit under a cabinet.

Coffee qualityIf you're passionate about coffee, look for a brewer that says it meets the Specialty Coffee Association's Golden Cup Standard. This means the coffee brews at what is regarded as the perfect time and temperature for the best cup of Joe.

But be aware that this standard calls for using 2 tablespoons of ground coffee for each 5-ounce cup, which produces a very full-bodied, strong cup of coffee that is not to everyone's taste.

Brewing coffee at home does mean you'll have a lot of spent grounds around, but instead of putting them in the trash, there are plenty of ways you can reuse old coffee grounds.

It has been revealed that cup sizeKeep in mind that coffee-maker cups are the equivalent of 5 ounces, or an old-fashioned teacup that isn't filled to the brim, leaving room for milk. Most coffee mugs in use today hold upward of 8 ounces. Therefore, a typical 12-cup coffee maker brews enough coffee for about seven mugs at the most.

What kind of carafe?Models with thermal carafes tend to be more expensive than those with glass carafes. You can bring thermal carafes to the table, where they'll keep coffee hot for refills. However, these carafes have narrow openings that are difficult to hand-wash, and most can't be cleaned in the dishwasher. However, thermal carafes are beneficial if you drink coffee throughout the day.

Milk frotherIf you prefer your coffee straight, you won’t be concerned about the milk frother option, although do consider that other household members or guests may prefer their coffee served with a smooth froth. Having a milk frother combined will also save you the issue of having a separate appliance on the countertop, taking up space.

Paper or permanent filters? Decide if you want to use a permanent filter or paper, disposable ones. Permanent filters are better for the environment, and you don't have to constantly replace them, but they do need to be thoroughly washed by hand and they tend to stain.

According to recent reports, also, it's easier to toss paper filters in the trash than knock grounds out of a metal filter. You may also find that the taste of the coffee produced differs depending on filter type and that you prefer one over the other.

Do you want to set it and forget it? With many machines, you can program them ahead of time to brew in the morning or right before you get home, and you can even set them to brew at the same time every day. But such features add to the price and work only if you take the time to read the manual and figure out how to use the setting.

If you're looking for a drip coffee maker, one of the best indicators of quality is an SCA Gold Cup Standard certification. The SCA (Specialty Coffee Association) awards this to machines that brew a 1:16 to 1:18 ratio (that's parts coffee to water) and within a specific temperature range of 196 and 205 degrees Fahrenheit.

Typically, machines that meet this specification are ideally designed to deliver a good cup of coffee. Every drip machine within this guide is SCA-certified, too.

Looking for an espresso machine? Don't pay much attention to the number of bars of pressure it offers. Anything over nine will suffice, as this is the amount of pressure required to make espresso. Instead, consider the number of grind settings on any included grinders, as a quality grinder should allow for plenty of customization. For most people, an in-built PID controller will assist you in getting that perfect extraction.

If you're looking for a bean-to-cup coffee machine, you're likely in the market for a superautomatic, meaning you can press a button and it will grind and brew your drink using fully automatic internal systems.

We've tested a number of bean-to-cup machines, and our top pick is the Terra Kafe Demi, which works fast and creates balanced, evenly-extracted brews. Its in-built milk frothing is also up to scratch if you enjoy a frothy coffee, although it'll never rival a hand-steamed latte.

In a recent development, if you want to create a range of milk-based espresso drinks, you should opt for something with a separate steam wand. I'd suggest you check out the Ninja Luxe Café Pro, which has a separate steam wand with both manual and automatic steaming.

According to recent reports, if you opt for automatic, the wand will texturize your milk to your desired level and according to the type of milk (dairy, oat, almond, etc) you choose. There's even a menu on the side of the machine which guides you through the different milk settings, and which to use depending on your desired drink.

My hot take is that you'll have a longer-lasting coffee setup if you opt for a separate brewer and one of the best coffee grinders, but if you want an in-built grinder, there are some good options out there.

Sources indicate that if you want an espresso machine, a quality grinder is especially key, as your beans will need to be ground very finely to achieve a quality extraction. As a general rule, I trust Breville machines to grind well, and I also had a great experience with the "Bean Adapt" tech in the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch.

#154131. Developing the perception to separate the form of a place from what it contains

Developing the perception to separate the form of a place from what it contains

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thedeletedscenes

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m on Virginia State Route 28, driving through Manassas and its neighboring town, Manassas Park.
  • Recent findings suggest that civil War heritage site and historic old town it is.
  • My journey starts at the beginning of the main commercial strip, near a microbrewery that sits on the property of what was once a racing-pigeon farm, and ends as the highway slims down and becomes the Old Town Manassas main street.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m on Virginia State Route 28, driving through Manassas and its neighboring town, Manassas Park. Most folks who aren’t from here probably know Manassas as a Civil War battle. Maybe as a historic town.

Recent findings suggest that civil War heritage site and historic old town it is. It’s also a good place to find great tacos.

My journey starts at the beginning of the main commercial strip, near a microbrewery that sits on the property of what was once a racing-pigeon farm, and ends as the highway slims down and becomes the Old Town Manassas main street. This commercial strip is about four miles that look like any place in America. Aging late-midcentury roadside suburban architecture, utterly dependent on cars, and worse for wear.

Recent findings suggest that but I find it striking. Places like this were at one time the newest, shiniest communities in America, with all of the modern postwar comforts. And today, they defy our inherited conceptions of suburbia.

Those who want suburbia to remain the domain of the affluent and upper-class may find suburban Manassas and Manassas Park too rundown and too poor. Those who love city life and support the redevelopment of aging suburbs may look askance at the dismal land use, the preponderance of parking lots, and the near-absence of public transit.

I admit those faults—would you want to walk on a sidewalk sandwiched between a highway and a retaining wall?—and while I’m happy that suburbia is open to people of all incomes and races, I also acknowledge that these places aren’t the most aesthetically pleasing.

But we sometimes imagine that the world is bounded by our ability to fully see it. This Manassas commercial strip is the kind of place for which we have not yet developed a language or an understanding. We don’t have a category for them. They are physically deteriorated, but they are not blighted. They are heavily populated and buzzing with commercial activity.

This commercial strip, and its adjacent residential neighborhoods, is probably most accurately understood not as a disorderly collection of deteriorating properties, but as an ethnic neighborhood, in the Chinatown or Little Italy mold.

Those old urban immigrant neighborhoods, though still lived in, have largely become tourist attractions or cultural curiosities—given a place in the American story they were not given in their heyday. They are no longer the sort of place where newly introduced immigrants actually begin their lives in America.

It has been revealed that had large numbers of Mexican and Latin American immigrants settled in American cities in the late 19th century, we’d have quaint old “Latin Towns” or “Little Mexicos” instead of legacy Little Italies and Chinatowns. Conversely, if Italian or Chinese immigrants were arriving today in the numbers they once did, they would probably be settling in the poorer and somewhat cast-off corners of suburbia. These places are performing, right now, a social and economic function analogous to one we already know how to recognize and celebrate in its historic form.

But for whatever reason—from the fact that suburban, car-oriented landscapes deteriorate rather than age gracefully, to the staying power of a cultural image, to, sadly, ethnic or racial animus—this recognition of rundown suburban commercial strips as cohesive, functional, even successful immigrant neighborhoods is not common, outside of people who take a particular interest in such things.

According to recent reports, the closest this phenomenon has gotten to mainstream is probably the bit of food-critic advice that the best and cheapest international food is found in a rundown strip mall. But why that is, and what it signifies, is not yet commonly understood or appreciated.

We should not wait until these places pass into the realm of “history,” remembered on our own terms and not actually experienced, to fully see and appreciate them. And we should work, right now, to see the spirit of these places, laboring beneath their form.

It has been revealed that this four-mile stretch of highway is one of those “Little Mexico” neighborhoods—or “Little El Salvador,” or some other name which doesn’t discriminate by country of origin. Manassas and Manassas Park are both roughly 45 percent Hispanic or Latino. And because people tend to self-sort by class if not ethnicity, some pockets of these towns are much more or less Hispanic.

I first stopped to take a look at the Megamart, a regional Hispanic grocery chain. The entrances have signs saying no photos or cameras. I complied, so I’ll just tell you what it looks like. It’s an old retail space, but well maintained, reminiscent of a Kmart interior.

There’s a food court with seating, a huge bakery display, the walls around the produce section festooned with piñatas for sale. In little spaces in the front, there are a few tiny businesses, including a sports jerseys and shoe store, and a mattress and bed store.

Out in the parking lot, there were a lot of folks sitting in cars or work vans, maybe waiting for a job or taking a break.

Recent findings suggest that A woman got out of her car and paced around the parking lot to take a phone call. A landscaping truck headed out for the highway. There’s nothing weird about it, but it strikes me how the parking lot takes on an element of public space here that is absent in more affluent communities. There are people around.

Just a little further down is another shopping center, with another former supermarket space; this one’s now a furniture store. It was once a “Marina” Safeway, a brand-centric building famous for its soaring, exposed-wood barrel-vault ceiling. (I could almost make out the barrel vault from the way they placed the drop ceiling.).

In that same strip, down at the end, there’s a row of Latino businesses, with a pho shop in the middle. There are bits and pieces where you could probably mistake this landscape for a snapshot of somewhere in Mexico or Latin America.

It has been revealed that I’m stopping for lunch at Tortilleria Sol de Dia, a Mexican barbecue joint in an old Pizza Hut. It’s notable enough to have gotten a little write-up in the regional lifestyle publication Northern Virginia Magazine.

However, despite that little boost, and despite being open for five years, it only has two Yelp reviews—and both in Spanish! That suggests that it isn’t really on the mental maps of a lot of people outside of the community.

There’s nothing left of a Pizza Hut inside; there’s a small market section, an ancient secondhand drink fridge, complete with a vintage woodgrain cabinet; a small seating area; and a little display of food, smoked and charred from the early morning hours over real wood, out in the back of the building in part of the old parking lot.

What to order? Carnitas, barbacoa, slices of soft, gelatinous pork skin, stacks of butterflied, char-grilled whole chickens and chicken leg quarters, whole fish, charred vegetables, homemade salsas and tortillas.

I was the only non-Hispanic customer in the place, and it was rather full. To my slight surprise, a fellow gringo who worked in the back overheard me trying to order, and explained to the lady at the counter what I wanted. The menu was in Spanish and English, but if not for me, there probably wouldn’t have been a lick of the latter.

Recent findings suggest that you shouldn’t expect this to be a revelation, or the best meal of your life. It’s food. It’s tasty, affordable, simple, and good. (If you should ever find yourself here, I’d skip the combo with average rice and beans, and stick to the delicious, smoky chicken, the carnitas, and the homemade salsas and tortillas.).

The scale of everything here is human. The smoker and piles of wood in the parking lot, the low ceiling, the building nestled into its little lot right along the highway. It can feel overcrowded and claustrophobic, I suppose.

But later, on my way home, I drove through the area’s newer commercial strip, about 10 minutes away. It boasts extra lanes of traffic—three on each side—larger stores and shopping centers set further back, at strange angles to the highway, behind meandering entrances and faux-landscaping retention ponds. It’s designed entirely for the speed and scale of the automobile. It feels stretched out, confusing, in some way lonely.

It has been revealed that there’s something about the tighter, older scale of development that shrinks social and emotional distance, too. Something about a little building you can just park a few feet from, and walk right up to, or around, or out back. Maybe it’s silly to get a little misty-eyed about an old corporate chain building showing its age. But these early suburban strips still have a touch of the proximity and the “good friction” that comes with tight, dense development. The pattern lends itself to flexibility and reinvention. I suspect the second life of the newer commercial strip will be more challenging, if it ever comes.

It has been revealed that I saved some room for dessert, because next door, in an old Captain D’s fast-food seafood restaurant, is La Michoacana, a Mexican ice cream and dessert shop (16 Yelp reviews). You can also go around the corner to Nathan’s Dairy Bar for old-school soft-serve at a seasonal stand. Maybe next time.

Sources indicate that for a little post-dessert walk, I browsed the H Mart just down the street, which has occupied an old Giant supermarket space for about 10 years. (Adding to the collection of reinvented fast-food buildings, I spotted an old Roy Rogers across the highway, which is now a Peruvian chicken joint.).

Recent findings suggest that H Mart is a Korean grocery chain which mostly stocks Korean and other Asian goods. However, this one has a considerable selection of Latin American foods. It’s quite nice inside. The pepper display was strikingly beautiful.

In a recent development, and just out of the frame, signs for “Korean Vegetable,” “Chinese Vegetable,” “American Vegetable,” “Indian Vegetable.” The huge Latino bakery section is next to a Korean food court. There’s a bar displaying a number of different Mexican cheeses. There’s an endcap, “Sale” in huge letters at the top, with Korean tissue boxes, above votive candles with images of the Virgin of Guadalupe and Santa Muerte (“Holy Death”).

Recent findings suggest that we might have some grand abstraction in mind when we talk about diversity or multiculturalism. This is what it actually looks like. This is America.

Industry observers note that there’s one more little stop, the last major commercial property before the old town. Unfortunately it’s a bit of a downer, a very old, half-vacant strip mall. One of the outparcels is a very neat-looking old Chinese restaurant, but it’s vacant too. What caught my eye here was a small Latino grocery store, whose sign has a little “Food-Rite” logo, a small regional grocer’s association, like IGA.

There was also a laundromat, with a neon sign indicating the age of the strip plaza: “Since 1957.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a long time. Long enough for a culture and a sense of place to mature, even amid the physical deterioration.

In some of these establishments, I might be the only white customer, or the only non-Hispanic customer. At times that can be a little bit uncomfortable. Not because I feel uncomfortable around Hispanics. It’s more like a feeling of, am I supposed to be here? Am I bothering the Mexican barbecue restaurant worker by trying to ask her what the food is or how to order, when she knows no more English than I do Spanish?

Recent findings suggest that both racism and respect could cause you to hold a place like this at a bit of an arm’s length, as if you’ve crossed some invisible border. This is a different place, not quite for you, whether because you don’t want to be here, or they don’t want you to be here, or you don’t know exactly how to be here.

Part of the reason I take these trips and write these pieces is to dispel that idea, for my readers, and frankly to some extent for myself. This is all right here. If it feels a world away, as it no doubt does to many people in more affluent surrounding communities, it is because it has never become a part of our mental maps. It is not because it is dangerous, exotic, unknowable, or off-limits.

Sources indicate that one of the most important “urbanist ideas”—I think of it as an urbanist idea, anyway—that I ever encountered was the idea that not everything has to be for you. So often we seem to think something like, “I don’t like X, therefore nobody should,” or even, “I don’t like X, therefore nobody does.” There is an implicit belief that the demand for things you don’t personally like is somehow not real.

It’s much healthier to accept that some things are just meant for a different audience, a different customer base, people at a different stage in their lives, people of different incomes or backgrounds. And that’s okay. There’s enough to go around. There’s enough room in this great major country for everybody.

It has been revealed that but the funny thing is that you might come to realize that, maybe, some of those things are for you. Maybe you’ll find that a taco truck between an auto shop and an off-brand convenience store is in fact your new favorite place to grab a bite. Maybe you’ll come to see a certain charm in the buzzing atmosphere of an aging but vibrant landscape like this. Maybe you’ll see what joins us—food, hospitality, work, everyday life, trying to make it—rather than what seems to separate us. Maybe there is more room and expansiveness in your perception than you thought there was.

When I say “urbanism,” I don’t mean perfectly dense, walkable, mixed-use communities, or I wouldn’t be writing about a late-midcentury commercial strip. I mean an idea. “Urbanism,” for me, is about living together with other people who may or may not quite be like you. It is about cultural sharing, bustling commerce, delight, community, peace.

And of course, food is one of the simplest and yet most deeply symbolic ways of sharing and offering. Take, eat.

According to recent reports, america prides itself on its culture of free enterprise. We claim to encourage entrepreneurship, hard work, multiple jobs, hustling, doing whatever it takes. But often, we seem to mean these things very abstractly. We turn up our noses at what that actually looks like.

In a recent development, it looks like multifamily houses, or multiple people splitting an old house. It looks like cheap old commercial buildings, sometimes roughly repurposed, housing a wide array of unique, local businesses. It looks like beater cars. It looks like biking and walking through landscapes that were not designed for cyclists and pedestrians. It looks like cracked, disused parking lots hosting food trucks and other informal businesses.

In a recent development, from the outside—and to those who no longer need it—it can look like disorganized chaos, like deterioration, like slow-motion collapse. In reality, some of what looks like this from the outside is precisely what sets the conditions for success.

Recent findings suggest that we thought we could make poverty disappear by trying to make it invisible. Instead of making it disappear, we multiplied it. We made it harder, in hundreds of little ways, to make a living. To hustle. To just up and do something with whatever you have, right now.

It has been revealed that we observed the things that poor or disfavored people did, and squeezed those things out. We pulled away the ladder to help people climb it. We mistake the means of escaping poverty for poverty itself.

There is poverty here, relatively speaking, anyway. Yet driving down this corridor, I feel a sense of energy and opportunity. A sense of climbing, of hope about the future. That’s part of what’s so striking about this world of scrappy entrepreneurship: it’s clear what you get at the other end. That clarity fades as you get richer, and it gets harder to grasp the next rung. It is difficult to distinguish an increase in hardship from an increase in expectations.

It has been revealed that these dusty stretches of obsolete first-generation sprawl have more culture and entrepreneurial hum in an inch than their shiny, sterile successors have in a mile. They are not imperfect versions of somewhere else or something else; they are successful places, and kinds of places, in their own right. And they are places where, quietly, American dreams are still being fashioned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Recent findings suggest that released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

Recent findings suggest that when a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are rapidly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating fresh crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, want more cynical diplomats, secret aims, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

Sources indicate that if you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that one of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and debuts a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

It has been revealed that nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that this might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.
