💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I bought the wrong espresso machine once, and it was an expensive mistake.
  • Now that I'm a Specialty Coffee Association-qualified barista, it's easy to see where I went wrong.
  • That's why I've put this guide together: it breaks down my tried-and-tested recommendations for the best espresso machines you can buy, but also walks you through the things you need to know before you buy a machine, as well as how to get the most out of each option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I bought the wrong espresso machine once, and it was an expensive mistake. With a taste for great coffee but limited knowledge of how to make it, I found one that looked good, had great reviews, and was on sale, and took the plunge. While it was a beautiful machine, it required far too much know-how for a newbie like me to get the most out of it.

Now that I'm a Specialty Coffee Association-qualified barista, it's easy to see where I went wrong. There are so many coffee makers on the market, and for the average first-time buyer, there's a lot of dense terminology to wade through.

That's why I've put this guide together: it breaks down my tried-and-tested recommendations for the best espresso machines you can buy, but also walks you through the things you need to know before you buy a machine, as well as how to get the most out of each option.

It has been revealed that there are three main types of domestic espresso machines — manual, automatic, and superautomatic — and each is suited to a different type of buyer. For confident home baristas who want a good machine and don't want to spend too much, the Breville Bambino will be your best friend. But if you want that extra bit of assistance, I think the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is the best espresso machine for most people.

Black Friday events are in full swing, which means there are plenty of deals on our favorite machines. We're keeping tabs on all the latest discounts in our best Black Friday deals roundup (and on plenty of other great tech we've tested). Or if you're holiday shopping, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers we recommend right now.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

If I was starting from scratch in my small kitchen, this is the machine I'd buy. The De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is strikingly compact and well-priced, but it doesn't skip out on smart features. Striking an ideal balance between user-friendly design and elevated touches, the La Specialista Touch walks you through every part of the brewing process with its responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen.

You can steam milk manually or use automatic features which this machine, which is a welcome feature that brings it into line with much more expensive options from the likes of Breville. In terms of cost, while it's an investment, I think the La Specialista Touch offers outstanding value.

It's fun to make espresso from scratch, but grinding, tamping and brewing can be a messy business. The La Specialista Touch doesn't have an in-built tamping arm, but it does include a tamping kit which allows you to check the volume of your grind and evenly compress it into a puck. The screw-on funnel helps keep things mess-free.

According to recent reports, the La Specialista Touch is super interactive, starting at the bean grinding settings. It uses De'Longhi's "Bean Adapt" tech, which walks you through the grinding process by asking you about the type of beans you're grinding and the color, which can indicate the roast level. Based on that, it asks you to set your grinder to a specific number, and then asks you to use the smart tamper to tell the machine the amount of coffee it needs to grind to get the perfect level.

Following all of that, the machine then tells you to increase of decrease grind size depending on how long the extraction takes. Combine all those factors, and it tackles the cause of most bad espressos right from the start.

Recent findings suggest that you can choose from 15 coarseness settings, which is pretty average for machines of this spec and price. It was capable of finely grinding light-roast beans, and there's plenty of scope to increase the grind size for darker roasts.

According to recent reports, I made some yummy espresso with the La Specialista Touch. It allows you to save bean settings to shortcut the Bean Adapt process, and I was able to flip between my go-to Lost Sheep Get To The Hopper beans and some cheap Aldi beans with ease.

When using great beans, the machine delivered a rich brew with notes of toffee and chocolate. It was the ultimate base for a latte or cappuccino, and if I was making an americano, I could leave my cup in place for the machine to top it up with hot water using a dispenser located right next to the group head.

I should also note that this machine makes cold brew, which is an increasingly popular feature in more modern machines. My brew was light, fruity, and balanced, but you should note that it doesn't brew cold espresso.

You can steam milk both manually and automatically with this machine, but I have a preference for manual steaming. Its included (useful) temperature gauge prevents your milk from burning, but it also gets in the way a little when hand-steaming. I got used to it, but it was a minor annoyance at first.

As for the automatic milk steaming, this was among some of the best I've tried. If I'm being picky, this is a feature I think Breville machines dominae, but the La Specialista Touch did make some fantastic latte milk which poured well with some swirling. My cappuccino foam was light and a little dry, which made a great topper to a shot of rich espresso.

We don't give out five-star reviews often, but Breville's cheapest coffee maker is hard to fault. Featuring the stainless steel exterior and quality construction we expect from Breville, it features a cost-conscious price tag that those familiar with the brand may not expect.

In a recent development, espresso machines can be chunky, so this is a rare compact option that will sit streamlined in just about any space. It's one of the few options in this guide that doesn't include a grinder, so you'll have to use pre-ground coffee or purchase your own grinder (check out our reviews of the best coffee grinders for some options, but they don't have to be expensive!) to use it.

Reviewer Erin stated "Damn, this is such a good machine. This machine’s functionality vs. cost is darn near unbelievable" when she tested it, and called the espresso she made in the Bambino "delectable".

This machine doesn't have a grinder, but it's worth digging into why that's not a bad thing. For a start, some enthusiasts prefer to buy separate grinders and espresso machines as it allows them to switch up their setup more easily, and if something breaks, you won't have to replace your entire coffee setup.

The machine comes with single-walled and double-walled baskets. If you initiative on using pre-ground coffee, I'd suggest starting with double-walled, as they can bring back some of the fresh and lively flavor you'll be missing from fresh-ground coffee.

The Breville Bambino produces very high-quality espresso without taking up too much counter space. Breville (or Sage, for European readers) is famed for making market-leading machines, and while this is one of the brand's entry-level options, it doesn't miss out on premium-feeling features or the powerful extraction you'll need to get a great shot.

There's pre-infusion, which will soak your puck to allow flavors to develop before extracting your shot, and there's also volumetric dispensing to pour either a single or double completely hands-free.

While you can get your barista on with this machine, it also comes with pressurized baskets, which will allow less finicky consumers to get a decent brew out of pre-ground beans.

In a recent development, unlike the Breville Bambino Plus, there's no automatic steaming with the Bambino. Reviewer Erin was sceptical of its one-hole steam wand — typically you'll be better off with a four-hole as it creates a higher level of pressure — but in testing, the Bambino had no trouble creating velvety-smooth milk.

The machine also comes with a milk jug, which is a nice bonus for an affordable machine, and its wand is more flexible than comparable machines from the likes of De'Longhi.

If you're on a budget, the De'Longhi Stilosa will be a good starting point. Admittedly, you'll need some skill to get great espresso out of this machine. This is because it's manual, meaning there are very few assisted features to make life easier. However, if you're willing to put in the work, the good news is that this machine is more than capable of extracting quality espresso, especially if you pair it with a quality grinder.

Sources indicate that considering the very reasonable price point, it's not surprising that this machine is mostly made of cheap-feeling plastic. But the good news is that under the hood, there's a decent brewer that performs as well as much more expensive machines.

Most impressive was its quality milk wand, which was capable of achieving a fine micro-foam that made delicious lattes and flat whites.

Industry observers note that this machine doesn't have a grinder. It's not too hard to make a decent manual espresso machine on a budget, but including a quality grinder (which is absolutely a non-negotiable if you care about great coffee) is expensive. Market-leading grinders can easily cost $300+, so if your machine offers both grinding and brewing capabilities for less than that, it's likely that the grinder is poor quality.

It has been revealed that so if you're on a budget and don't mind getting hands-on, the De'Longhi Stilosa is a good work around. Especially if you combine it with a quality hand-grinder like the sub-$100 1Zpresso Q Air.

Tested by our reviews writer (and former barista) Erin, the De'Longhi Stilosa competed with some of the much more premium machines she's reviewed.

With a bit of experimentation and dedication, she found that there’s no reason why you can’t pull consistently delicious shots on the Stilosa. It does require a little know-how, but that's a classic trade-off for the price.

According to recent reports, because the machine doesn't brew to single or double shots, you need to monitor and switch it off yourself. For this, you'll be better off buying a coffee scale so you can tailor your ratios.

You might expect the steam wand on a cheap machine to be flimsy, but if anything, Erin found that the Stilosa’s steam wand can be a touch overzealous.

A former barista, Erin knows her way around a steam wand, and she found that this one needed full concentration during steaming to prevent the milk from becoming over-textured.

However, she did make some awesome lattes in the Stilosa. And for the price, it's one of the top steam wands she's tested.

The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is designed around automation, handling weighing, dosing, and grind adjustment for you, so if you're new to home espresso, it removes much of the guesswork. We found its auto-grind-size calibration especially helpful, letting us lock in consistent results with barely any trial and error. This built-in guidance helps streamline the process for beginners, and it's often the number one reason friends and family tell me their machine doesn't work properly. It does, dad, you've just got the wrong grind size. With the Mini Plus, auto-grind-size calibration makes dialing in much easier for new owners, so you can reliably pull good shots without trial-and-error adjustments.

Recent findings suggest that with both automatic and manual milk options, the Mini Plus lets you choose how hands-on you want to be. This is especially helpful for beginners learning to texture milk at their own pace.

Compared to the more advanced De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, which provides guided tamping and more complex brewing modes, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus stands out for its simplicity and compact footprint. While it lacks in-built tamping and step-by-step drink guidance, it offers a straightforward way to start making espresso at home without requiring a lot of counter space or a steep learning curve.

Something that really sets Ninja coffee makers apart is that their grinder works on an unusual weight-based system. That's the best way, in theory, to ensure you're getting your espresso ratio right every time, and it's why some coffee fanatics will pre-weigh their beans before feeding them into a coffee machine.

The Mini Plus does lack in-built tamping, which is something you'll find in more premium models from Ninja, but it does have a dosing funnel which allows you to catch every drop from the grinder and minimize countertop mess.

Reviewer Erin enjoyed the coffee she made with this machine, but it didn't blow her socks off. She described it as akin to chain coffee shop coffee, which is no bad thing, because the average coffee machine buyer simply wants to replicate their favorite to-go drink at home. But if you know your arabica from your robusta, it might not hit the mark.

There are some pros and cons to the milk steaming with the Ninja Luxe Café line. The milk jug has an in-built spinner to create a vortex in the jug when you're using the automated steaming mode, but you can use the wand manually if you want to learn how to steam by hand.

A big bonus for those who drink a range of milk types is that if you opt for pre-set milk steaming, you can switch between plant and dairy milk settings to prevent oat or soy milk from burning.

This is a halfway house between traditional milk steaming and using a handheld frother to create artificial bubbles in your coffee. Personally, I prefer the automated steam wands you'll find on Breville machines like the Bambino Plus.

But the in-built spinner does have one big bonus in allowing you to create cold foam to pair with your cold coffee. This is something I've not seen in any of the other espresso machines on the market.

It has been revealed that if you want a hands-off espresso machine that delivers consistently excellent shots, the Terra Kaffe Demi is a confident pick. The main advantage of superautomatic machines is that they make your coffee from scratch with the touch of a button, but when testing these machines, we frequently find that the finished cup just tastes... bad. That's not an concern reviewer Dan had with the Demi, which allowed him to dial in his perferred settings for espresso and long black coffee, and delivered a consistently delicious brew, cup after cup.

Under the hood, the Demi automates the entire espresso process, from grinding with its conical burr grinder to dosing, tamping, and brewing. In testing, the shots came out reliably rich every single time. Plus, it looks fantastic, and packs in a lot of smarts without being too in-your-face about it.

The main downside is that there's no in-built milk frother. But we tend not to rate the milk frothers which come with superautomatic machines, anyway. You can buy Terra Kaffe's standalone milk frother separately, and use it to make everything from cappuccino to cold foam. The other main concern Dan encountered was that the water tank was on the small side at 47 fluid ounces.

In a recent development, the Demi comes with conical burr grinders, which are typically a better pick than flat burr grinders due to their quieter operation and more consistent results. Because it's hidden away, we tend to find that manufacturers can cut corners when making the grinders for automatic espresso machines, so it's immediately a positive sign that the Demi features conical burrs.

What's less promising is the limited range of grind settings: from one through to five, which is significantly less than the 30+ settings you'll find from alternatives like the Breville Oracle Dual Builer.

The Demi can make five drinks: Espresso, Lungo, Americano, Drip, and Hot Water. So, make that four coffee drinks. It's not the most versatile pick, but in testing we found that our espresso was lively and, most importantly, consistently good.

Dan, a noted coffee snob, remarked "I was genuinely surprised at how consistent the shots are. Once I had my temperature, strength, and volume dialed in, the shots were as close to perfect as you could expect every time I hit the button.".

Recent findings suggest that there's no milk frother here. Instead, you'll have to buy the newly-released Aero Milk Frother if you want a companion to turn your espresso into a cappuccino.

The latest premium contender from Fellow, the Espresso Series 1, is engineered for buyers who want café-level control at home—offering deep shot profile customization and a steam wand that could make a barista blush. If you’re the kind of person who tweaks pre-infusion, flow rate, or pressure profiles for each roast, you’ll be right at home here; the steam wand with its versatile ball joint is a standout for microfoam and serious cappuccino work.

In our testing, dialing in shots with the Series 1 felt more like sculpting than brewing. The results spoke for themselves: the espresso came through with a distinct sweetness and bright acidity that made it hard not to drink the entire shot at once. This isn’t just theoretical control—it’s the real, tangible difference you can taste in the cup, shot after shot.

In a recent development, but there’s a trade-off. Compared to something like the De’Longhi La Specialista Touch, which is more compact and user-friendly, the Series 1 leans into complexity and countertop presence. It’s best for buyers who want to experiment, customize every variable, and don’t mind a learning curve (or a bigger footprint). If that’s you, there’s no better playground—but if you want guided simplicity or a tidier setup, look elsewhere.

There's no built-in grinder with the Fellow Espresso - you'll have to provide your own. Enthusiasts willing to spend the $1.5k to buy this machine likely have a grinder they're happy with already, but if you're building your set-up from scratch, be aware that your budget will have to allow for a grinder as well as brewing device, unless you buy an all-in-one coffee maker.

Recent findings suggest that you can let the Fellow do the heavy lifting when brewing, giving you automatic profiles and step-by-step instructions for brewing that you select with the built-in LCD screen. Or you can dive into the exhaustive settings menu and sort things yourself. Whichever way you want to do it, you'll end up with some awesome brews.

Industry observers note that one small complaint we have is the machine's tendency to leave you with wet pucks of coffee grounds once you're finished making your drink. It's not a massive problem, but in theory the Fellow has the technology to produce dry, easily disposable pucks like most other espresso machines of this price.

Recent findings suggest that the steam wand on the Fellow Espresso is one of the best in the business. In fact it produced the single best result we've ever seen for non-dairy milk. It's the kind of milk results that no other machine we know of can match.

Just watch out for the auto-purge function though. It can get in the way of cleaning if you know what you're doing.

It has been revealed that most of this guide is geared towards the average home brewer, but if you want to take it to the next level, the Gaggia Classic E24 is our recommendation. It was tested by our Reviews Editor Peter, a former chef and serious coffee-lover who doesn't mind taking the time to craft coffee the old-fashioned way. His main gripe was that it came with poor-quality tools, but these are easily replaced.

This machine lacks a lot of the assists you'll find with Breville and De'Longhi machines. There's no PID, no thermoblock, and you'll have to start and stop the extraction yourself.

Sources indicate that the plus side of this is that you get complete control over your shot of coffee. Some machines try and steer you because they assume they know better, but if you've got the know-how, this machine will leave you to it and not intervene.

It has been revealed that there's no grinder to be seen here. You'll want to pair this compact espresso machine with a quality home grinder such as the Eureka Mignon Specialita, which just so happens to be the grinder we used during testing.

Recent findings suggest that as I stated, this machine leaves all the hard work to you. It's a single-boiler without a PID. What does this mean? Well, it heats up the entire tank instead of the amount of water needed for a specific dose, and it won't monitor and adjust the temperature of your coffee during extraction. You can add a PID if you choose to modify this machine, but if you go as is, you're temperature-surfing to hit the optimum extraction.

Sources indicate that due to its larger brass boiler and brass group head, the Gaggia now offers higher levels of temperature stability (a common problem in machines without PID). Peter found that it was more than capable of extracting complex, punchy espresso. "I tested the Gaggia with a range of beans, including light-medium, medium and dark roasts, using washed, wet-hulled, honey-processed and natural processing. The E24 did justice to the lot.".

In a recent development, peter made some brilliant lattes in this machine. Its steam wand is more powerful than any other in this guide (aside perhaps from the Meraki), because (like a commercial machine) it works with a boiler to hit high pressure on demand.

Recent findings suggest that this means you'll be able to create glossy microfoam for a flat white or cappuccino in a matter of seconds. Peter found that it could make a flat white in ten seconds flat. However, as you're working with one boiler, you'll need to 'purge' your machine to get rid of the overheated water after milk steaming is finished. The temperature will be too high to go back to brewing espresso.

In a recent development, I'm pretty cagey with who I let review espresso machines for Tom's Guide. When I bought my first espresso machine, I couldn't tell if my failure to get a good espresso out of my fancy new gadget was the machine's fault, or human error. If I'd written a review of that machine, it wouldn't have been very fair on the reader, or the machine!

But now I've got five years of testing, well over 30 coffee machine reviews, and a Specialty Coffee Association qualification under my belt. My friends are always asking me questions about coffee, why their machine isn't working for them, or which they should buy, so I'd like to think I can be that person to our readers, too.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, at Tom's Guide, I'm not alone. We've got a brilliant team of experienced testers with almost 20 years of coffee expertise between us.

As a former barista (and current product tester), I've spent a lot of time getting hands-on with espresso machines.

After a combined three years at two of the biggest coffee chains and a year at an artisan independent coffee shop, I can detect a well-balanced shot when I taste it, and can also interpret the culprit behind a poor extraction, be it low pressure, grind size, or poor temperature controls.

Spending three years making hundreds of coffees a day might make a person gag at the sight of lattes, but coffee still holds a special place in my heart.

My favorite drink is an oat milk flat white, made with Kenyan or Ethiopian beans.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

Recent findings suggest that as a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

Fun fact: every job I’ve held since has given me access to espresso machines — oddly enough, that includes when I worked at an energy company, where we had a commercial Expobar machine plumbed into the office kitchen!

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, espresso machines.

Sources indicate that I’ve used home espresso machines from Breville/Sage, Rancilio, Gaggia, De’Longhi, Diletta and more. Through my years of testing (and tasting), I have the experience to know when a machine performs as it should and whether or not it’s worth your hard-earned cash.

We test a ton of coffee gear at Tom's Guide, and not everything can make it to the final guide. If I don't include something, that doesn't necessarily mean we don't recommend it, so if none of the machines listed above take your fancy, you might get along better with one of these tried-and-tested options.

KitchenAid KF8 Coffee Machine (★★★★☆).

Sources indicate that we don't tend to rate superautomatic espresso machines, but the KF8 surprised us. In fact, it used to feature in this guide until we tested the Terra Kaffe Demi.

Read the full KitchenAid KF8 Coffee Machine review.

Casabrews Ultra Coffee Machine (★★★★☆).

If you're on a budget, Casabrews machines are worth a look. The trade-off is in the built quality, but in our tests, we did find that they're capable of making a tasty espresso.

Read the full Casabrews Ultra Coffee Machine review.

Meraki Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

According to recent reports, newcomer to the espresso game Meraki is offering a stunning range of features for the price. The downside? It's still in development, with some tweaks having now been made to the model we first tested, which means we can't recommend it until we've tested the fresh and improved model.

Read the full Meraki Espresso Machine review.

The De’Longhi Dedica Duo is neat and compact, but it's quite expensive for what it is, especially when the Stilosa is cheaper and just as capable. However, you can't deny that it's a looker, which could make it a contender if you're setting up a coffee nook.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo review.

Industry observers note that our love of the Breville Bambino Plus is very well documented, but when we added its cheaper counterpart, the Bambino, to this guide, we felt that we didn't need both here. The Plus is incredible, with automated steaming and powerful extraction, but it's slightly less good value for money.

Read the full Breville Bambino Plus review.

De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo (★★★★☆).

Looking for a budget-friendly espresso machine with character and an in-built grinder? The De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo is practically in a league of its own, offering specs that punch well above its weight. The only reason it's not in this guide is that we love the Specialista Touch more.

Read the full De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo review.

KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

Sources indicate that the KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine with Burr Grinder is the entry-level option in KitchenAid's line of coffee makers. It's a mid-price, high-quality option, but it lacks a lot of the automated features you'll see from options like Breville and De'Longhi.

Read the full KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine review.

According to recent reports, with some trial and error though, Reviews Editor Peter hit his stride with the Silvia. After some experimentation he stated he was "actually a little taken aback at how nice espresso shots tasted." If you've got a refined palate and espresso known-how, this could be a good option.

Read the full Rancilio Silvia (V6) Espresso Machine review.

De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆).

Industry observers note that the De'Longhi Dedica Duo is a good espresso machine capable of making pleasant cold brew for just $299. Even so, it's the same price as the fantastic Breville Bambino and $150 pricier than our favorite budget machine, the De’Longhi Stilosa.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine review.

Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆).

The Philips Barista Brew is Philips' first attempt at an automatic coffee machine. The rest of the line is superautomatic, and start at quite affordable prices. When we tested the Barista Brew, we didn't have an issue with the quality of its extraction or construction, it just struggles to break through the very crowded market of machines that look, cost, and perform almost exactly the same.

Read the full Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine review.

According to recent reports, you probably didn't come to this guide looking for a wireless coffee maker, but this non-electric option is very affordable, super portable, and ideal for travel. It uses a valve to create the pressure needed to extract espresso, and we were really impressed by how well it worked.

Read the full Wacaco Minipresso review.

The Terra Kaffe is super smart. It claims to feature AI tech that will personalize your brew to your specific preferences, and it certainly looks space-age. The price will rule it out of contention for most people though, and it's also a very large option.

Read the full Terra Kaffe TK-02 review.

Philips 3200 Series LatteGo (★★★☆☆).

Recent findings suggest that the Philips 3200 Series LatteGo is one of the most affordable superautomatic espresso machines on the market. It feels plasticky in use and the milk dispenser will struggle to compete with more expensive options, but if you want a one-and-done option that doesn't cost the earth, it's a good choice.

Read the full Philips 3200 Series LatteGo review.

You can make any kind of coffee drink you like with this automatic machine from Ninja, but the mixed quality of the outputs prevented us from awarding a higher rating.

Read our full Ninja AutoBarista Pro review.

Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series (★★☆☆☆).

Sources indicate that one to avoid this time around — it makes coffee, but there's not much to say about it. It costs far too much money for the quality of espresso that it spits out, even if the device itself does look pretty special.

Read the full Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review.

Recent findings suggest that we review a lot of espresso machines at Tom's Guide. Very few of them make it into our buying guides, but you can see a comprehensive list of other models we've tested at the bottom of this guide.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to testing espresso machines, there's a lot of room for human error. In order to minimize this, I work closely with a team of true coffee experts, from former baristas to serious home baristas. Every review you'll read on Tom's Guide will be from a true espresso enthusiast who can tell their flat whites from their cappuccinos and their arabica from their robusta.

Industry observers note that we consider a huge range of factors when evaluating espresso machines. Here's a non-exhaustive list of the things we test for:.

Ease of use: You shouldn't have to be a pro to work an espresso machine. These appliances are designed to make life easier, so while it's fair to expect a learning curve if you opt for a manual machine with lots of hands-on features, we mark machines down for any quirks or fiddly features that will make day-to-day use harder for the average buyer.

Ease of cleaning: Some machines are splashy, messy, and get greasy from the touch of a button. These are workhorses, sure, but they're also meant to look nice, so we evaluate whether they spill grounds, splatter milk, or will require any major upkeep with each review.

Value for money: Even a budget espresso machine can be expensive, so we always consider whether a machine is priced competitively when putting it to the test. If we wouldn't recommend our friends spend their money on a machine, we wouldn't recommend it to you, either.

According to recent reports, grinding: If a machine has an in-built grinder, we put it through the same testing that we use when evaluating the best coffee grinders. After all, the quality of your grinder plays a massive part in achieving a good extraction. It's the single most key part of any espresso-brewing process. We evaluate the range of grind sizes on offer with every machine (you'll want a very fine consistency, but this will vary depending on the bean you use), as well as how much coffee a machine grinds automatically. A lot of enthusiasts brew using ratios, so we like to weigh the grounds before we brew for good measure.

Industry observers note that brewing: Albeit an key step, this is also the simplest to test. Whether a machine can brew well is dependent on the performance of the grinder, but we know we've got a quality coffee if it brews at that sweet spot between 190 to 200°F (88 and 93°C) and we get between 25-30ml of espresso. We use a coffee scale to test this, just to be extra thorough.

Taste test: Metrics aside, it's all in the taste-test. We buy high-quality coffee (currently, we're using a subscription to Hard Lines' specialty coffee) that's freshly-roasted to give our machines the best possible chance of brewing a brilliant espresso. And if it tastes too bitter or too tart, we know it's not the beans' fault! If the coffee tastes too grassy, it suggests the machine doesn't brew hot enough, and if it's burnt-tasting, that's a sign that it's not got good temperature regulation and is scorching our grounds.

Milk steaming: Steam wands need to be powerful, ergonomic and responsive. A great wand will not only heat your milk but also help to create a powerful vortex, which will add texture and incorporate air into your milk jug. I'll get more into how to use a steam wand below, but you best believe that if former barista Erin can't get a good texture from a steam wand, there's no hope for a home user.

Super-automatic espresso machines will often feature milk dispensers that automatically froth your milk and pour it into your mug. This is really convenient if you don't like the idea of learning to steam milk by hand, but just so we're clear, these machines don't steam your milk. They simply heat it and inject some bubbles as they pour into your cup. It gets the job done, but it's not going to compete with a coffee shop-quality flat white.

Longevity: You need to be prepared to look after an espresso machine. They block easily if you don't descale regularly, and your group head and steam wand will need to be flushed out periodically. This aside, we've also tried machines that simply don't feel like they're built to last. Where possible, we like to hang onto a top pick for prolonged home use and testing. That way, we can update our guide if it doesn't seem built to last. Our number one, the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera, is currently living with Erin as her home machine, allowing us to continue to evaluate its position in this guide.

It has been revealed that this question used to be a lot more simple to answer: there's manual, and there's super-automatic! However, things have changed a lot in the last few years, and now there's an increasing number of machines that sit somewhere in between.

In truth, it would be easier to characterize types of espresso machine as a spectrum, all the way from lever pump machines like La Pavoni to one-touch super-automatics like Jura.

But to make life easier, I've divided the domestic machines in this guide into three categories:.

Espresso machines are pretty complicated, which is why I did a dedicated Specialty Coffee Association course before compiling this guide. While I’ve tried to make it as accessible as possible, there is some terminology you might need to learn to understand the reviews below. Here are the ABC's of espresso machines.

If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: “how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this?".

I posed this question to Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni. “It’s quite simple really, it’s all about extracting the flavor from your coffee,” she told me.

It has been revealed that “There’s a scientific process for making an espresso. It has to be between 88 and 93°C [190 to 200°F], you have to put about 9 bars of pressure on it, and you want to extract between 25 and 30ml of liquid. So what all these machines do is offer a way of controlling that process.”.

Sources indicate that there are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso. This includes the beans you use, how you grind them, the volume of grounds in your portafilter, the pressure you use when tamping, the temperature stability of your machine, the water pressure exerted, the volume of water pushed into your puck… that’s a non-exhaustive list, and it’s before we even get into milk steaming!

There are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso.

It has been revealed that here’s what I wish I’d known when I bought my first espresso machine: The more automated features you opt for, the fewer variables you’ll need to worry about. “Sometimes with espresso machines, an entry-level price will actually require more skill,” claims Dunstan.

“If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this? So you’re either someone who doesn’t have a lot of time to spend on making your coffee, or you want to delve into that world where you’re getting hands-on.".

According to recent reports, there's an unfortunate irony with espresso machines. You can get good espresso with a cheaper machine, but to do so, you'll need to learn the ins and outs of how these machines work. For the entry-level buyer without much knowledge, you'll often have to spend a lot more on a super-capable machine that will take all the hard work out of the equation.

It doesn't make much sense, right? Coffee enthusiasts can get away with spending $200 on a basic espresso machine because they've got the skill to use it properly, but if you're just dipping your toes in the water? Well, prepare to spend at least $500. It's no wonder why so many people opt for a pod machine like a Keurig or a Nespresso!

Industry observers note that fortunately, the market is catching up. An increasing amount of espresso machines feature assisted settings that will remove some of the variables that can mess up your espresso. This includes automated grinding that controls the volume of coffee dispensed into your portafilter, automated tamping for an even pressure, and even hands-free steam wands that will texture your milk for you.

The majority of the machines I've included in this machine fit into this automatic category in some sense. I think they're the best option for most people, allowing you to learn as you use the machine and get hands-on if you wish, but also taking the reins when you just want a low-effort espresso.

You'll see in the products included I've mentioned how many bars of pressure they each have, but what does this mean, and does it even matter? Well, the short answer is no. You won't necessarily see a better extraction from a machine with 20 bars over a machine with 15. This is because the ideal pressure needed for espresso is 9 bars.

According to recent reports, I asked Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, to explain the significance of pressure for espresso machines. "You want to hit 9 bars for optimal extraction," he told me.

Industry observers note that "If the pressure is too low, you'll bring out grassy flavors. The pressure won't bring out the sugars from your beans.

"Too high, and your coffee will have a bitter, burnt taste.".

If all you need to make a great espresso is 9 bars of pressure, so I asked Lane why so many espresso machines have more?

Industry observers note that "Think of it like a car," Lane told me. "You don't want to drive it at top speed all the time, but driving in a comfortable range of what your car is capable of will mean it's not constantly being run flat-out.".

He explained that despite the maximum pressure of any machine, they'll use OPVs (which stands for over pressure valves) to keep espresso extraction running at a consistent 9 bars of pressure.

So, while higher pressure doesn't necessarily mean a machine is any better, you might not want to buy a machine with a maximum output of 9 bars, or it could lead to a shorter lifespan for your machine.

Most espresso machines will come with four baskets: two single and two double, with a mix of double-walled and single-walled constructions. I'll explain the difference between single-walled and double-walled below, but what's the significance of your basket size and capacity?

Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, explained it to me: "There are two main basket widths: 54mm, which features on Sage / Breville's Barista range, and 58mm, which features on our Jet range.".

"58mm is considered to be commercial-grade. The larger and shallower basket will give you marginally better results because you're more easily able to permeate all of the grounds inside your basket.".

After testing countless espresso machines, I don't think my palette is quite so attuned that I could turn my nose up at an espresso from a 54mm basket. But it's useful to know if you want to replace or upgrade any parts of your machine what size portafilter baskets the group head will fit.

Single-walled and double-walled baskets, also known respectively as unpressurized and pressurized, are included with your espresso machine to give you options. As a general rule of thumb, you'll get better results from a pressurized basket if you're using pre-ground coffee. It will help you overcome some of the shortcomings of a grind size that's too coarse, or coffee that's less fresh. But if you want to taste the authentic flavor of your fresh-ground beans, a single-walled basket is the way to go.

In our reviews, we always use fresh-ground coffee, so we stick to single-walled baskets for the majority of our testing.

According to recent reports, when I asked him to explain how pressurized baskets work, Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, mentioned "Think of a group of people running down a hall and having to go through a door." He explained, "That's what the double-walled basket does. It creates pressure by restricting the flow of your coffee, forcing it to build up more flavor and crema than you'd have been able to achieve with a less fresh coffee.".

We've done a thorough explainer on this in our guide to pressurized coffee baskets — how do they work and when should you use them? The short answer? They can act as a cheat code to a better espresso if you're not working with the ideal gear, but a machine with an in-built grinder shouldn't need one.

The vast majority of domestic espresso machines use thermoblock technology to heat water on demand. But how does it work, and what are the pros and cons?

Recent findings suggest that there are very few single boiler machines on the market, but the Rancilio Silvia is one of them. Boiler machines will heat your water and keep it at temperature for as and when you decide to use it. A single-boiler uses one boiler for both the group head and the steam wand, which require different temperatures and therefore will need to you purge excess hot water as you use different elements of the machine.

Recent findings suggest that dual boilers have one boiler for the group head, and another for your steam wand. They're not super popular for domestic, and I've not included a dual-boiler in this guide. They have a higher energy consumption because they keep your water hot for more precision and stability.

Industry observers note that what about thermoblock? I asked Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni, to explain. “A thermoblock is a heated metal block with one or more pipes running through it that will rapidly heat water on demand," she explained.

"They’re usually very compact so they don’t take up much space, meaning they can be fitted in smaller machines, and they’re more energy efficient [than a dual boiler].”.

Recent findings suggest that “So the advantage is that they’re fast, small, and energy-efficient. The disadvantage is that they offer less temperature consistency than a dual boiler machine.

"And they can, over time, be susceptible to limescale, so they may not last as long. Whereas if you buy a dual boiler La Pavoni machine, and you look after it, I’d expect it to last you a lifetime.”.

10 Hacks Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far.
  • I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are key.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are key. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

Recent findings suggest that if you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

Using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having stated that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

In a recent development, haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an issue where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a massive problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That said, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift issues in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Industry observers note that committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area quickly.

According to recent reports, if you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same problems, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently shows a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.

According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Recent findings suggest that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

\(\langle \mathrm{lap},q\rangle\) is the Laplacian of \(q\) evaluated at \(x = y = 0\).

Instead of applying a simple differential operator to a complicated expression, we are applying a complicated differential operator to a simple expression. No matter how complicated an expression \(p\) we apply, the intermediate results of applying it to \(q\) are always bounded in complexity. For example in this case we are only ever going to get linear combinations of.

Recent findings suggest that and that's it. Anything else that pops up is just going to be a linear combination of these. Which means that if we're interested in computing the Laplacian in 2D we only ever need to track 4 coefficients. We don't need to keep track of the full Hessian. In fact we can replace the polynomial on the right of the pairing with a 4-vector and replace apply with code to act directly on that representation.

Sources indicate that we have just rediscovered the method for computing Laplacians I described many years ago at Computing errors with square roots of infinitesimals. But now it's more general and we can use this for any constant differential operator. For example the biharmonic operator corresponds to the polynomial \((\sum_i x_i^2)^2\). When you compute all of the possible expressions that can arise from applying the \(\partial_i\) operator it forms a far smaller space than you might get from naively carrying along the power series up to degree 4.

Recent findings suggest that after I proposed my original Laplacian method it was eventually rediscovered and turned into well-optimized code at folx. It's used in many places such as PINNs and VMC.

Compare also with this paper: Collapsing Taylor Mode Automatic Differentiation.

ChatGPT keeps wanting to turn this into a subject called apolar algebra (which highlights that many AD problems were solved over a century ago) but the key construction there is a quotient and quotients are hard to work with.

FWIW I fully embrace our new AI overlords but I actually wrote all of this myself giving Codex the role of formatting it for blogger.com.

According to recent reports, I need to mention that the idea that you can flip the role of differentiator and differentiated expression plays a major role in quantum mechanics. And lastly, this pairing is central to umbral calculus.

It has been revealed that sierra, the AI agent company co-founded by OpenAI chair Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed. That is almost double the $15.8B it was valued at in May, and it indicates annual recurring revenue has passed $400M.

Sierra, the AI customer service firm led by Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, it unveiled on Monday. Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners are leading the round.

The valuation is almost double the $15.8B Sierra was worth in May, when it raised $950M. All of its previous lead investors, including Benchmark, Sequoia and Tiger Global, are investing again.

Sources indicate that sierra builds AI agents that answer customers’ calls and messages for large companies. It says its annual recurring revenue passed $400M in October, just over two and a half years after launch. Almost half of the Fortune 50 are customers, it says.

Sierra charges for outcomes, such as a resolved problem or a paid insurance claim, rather than per seat or per token, and Zendesk is moving the same way. Insurer Guardian recently handed it 1 million dental calls a year, and its agents can now take card payments through Stripe.

According to recent reports, taylor, who also chairs OpenAI’s board, co-founded Sierra with former Google executive Clay Bavor. In a blog post, the pair addressed fears of an AI bubble.

“We’re seeing some of the oldest, most regulated companies in the world deploy AI the fastest,” they wrote. They pointed to last week’s record Anthropic IPO as a sign of how fast AI is moving.

Competition in AI customer service is heating up. In June, Salesforce agreed to buy support-AI firm Fin for $3.6B.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:58PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than CrowdStrike ›.

Sources indicate that crowdStrike (CRWD -8.92%) declared on Monday that it will buy Zscaler (ZS +17.67%) in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion. The press release put the offer at $260.41 per Zscaler share, a 34% premium to Friday's close.

Sources indicate that but Zscaler holders won't receive $260.41 in cash. They will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share, a fixed ratio that rises and falls with CrowdStrike's price. The $260.41 figure comes from CrowdStrike's Friday close of $229.44.

It has been revealed that by 3:30 p.m. ET Monday, CrowdStrike had dropped 9.6% to $207.45. At that price, 1.135 shares are worth about $235.45, roughly $25 less than the headline number. Zscaler traded at $227.45, up 16.8% on the day but still $8 below the deal's current value.

CrowdStrike reported its third-quarter results alongside the deal. Revenue rose 28% to $1.58 billion. Net fresh annual recurring revenue reached a record $419 million, and total annual recurring revenue grew 27% to $6.26 billion.

The stock fell anyway, losing about $22 billion in market value, which is half the price CrowdStrike agreed to pay. Paying in stock means CrowdStrike's current shareholders give up part of the company: they will own about 84.1% of the combined business, and Zscaler's holders 15.9%.

CrowdStrike says the deal will add about $1 billion in annual revenue within 30 months of closing and cut about $500 million in yearly costs within 18 to 24 months. It prepares to sell its Falcon products to about 8,000 Zscaler customers that don't use CrowdStrike today.

In a recent development, the merger filing needs approval from Zscaler shareholders and antitrust regulators. The companies expect to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, which runs from August 2027 to January 2028. Either side can walk away if the deal hasn't closed by Nov. 23, 2027, a date that moves to Feb. 23, 2028, if only antitrust or foreign-investment reviews remain.

Industry observers note that founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry and his affiliates, who hold about 34% of Zscaler's shares, have agreed to vote in favor of the deal. Zscaler would owe CrowdStrike a $1.4 billion fee if it walked away for a better offer.

It has been revealed that A 3.5% gap for a wait of a year or more is small, which suggests traders expect the deal to close. It also means Zscaler's stock now mostly tracks CrowdStrike's. Anyone buying Zscaler at $227 is effectively betting on CrowdStrike's price in late 2027 among cybersecurity stocks, and that price has already fallen 26% from its 52-week closing high of $278.86 on Oct. 6.

Sources indicate that zscaler holders who want to own the combined company can hold on. Those who bought Zscaler for its own business should know that, if the deal closes, they will end up owning CrowdStrike stock.

The best Black Friday deals on Asics running shoes available right now are mostly on last-gen shoes, but this is no bad thing.

I've been testing running shoe for a decade and often recommend buying the previous model of popular shoes, because brands frequently only make minor updates to the latest version so you get better value on last-gen sneakers in sales.

That’s certainly the case with many top Asics shoes in the current Black Friday sales, and as I have tested both the latest and past models of popular picks like the Novablast, Gel-Nimbus and Gel-Kayano I can tell you what you are — and aren’t — missing out on by getting an older shoe.

The Sonicblast wasn't a hugely popular launch last year, which I guess means Asics has a lot of stock to sell in sales now the Sonicablast 2 has come out, because this is a great price. It's a plated trainer with a firm, fast ride that's good for workouts, and best paired with a more comfortable option like the Novablast in a running shoe rotation.

Recent findings suggest that the Cumulus is a more affordable alternative to the Gel-Nimbus in the Asics line-up, but offers a similarly comfortable and versatile ride for your daily training. I think the Gel-Nimbus 27 is better value than the Gel-NImbus 28 in the sales right now thanks to this deal. It has a smooth, comfortable ride, and the newer Gel-Cumulus 28 isn't a major upgrade based on my testing.

It has been revealed that the Gel-Kayano is Asics' flagship stability running shoe, offering extra support for overpronators on the run. I've tested the newer Asics Gel-Kayano 33, and while it has some notable updates, I still rate the Gel-Kayano 32 the better buy thanks to this deal.

Industry observers note that I still have hope that we'll see the Novablast 5 drop to lower prices than this in the sales, but this is still a decent deal on an excellent running shoe. I prefer the Novablast to the Nimbus and Cumulus myself because it's a little lighter and livelier at any pace. While the Asics Novablast 6 is an excellent upgrade the Novablast 5 remains a great daily trainer worth considering at this lower price.

I've just wrapped up my testing of the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29, which is quite a lot softer than the 28 thanks to a newly introduced midsole foam. I'm not entirely sure which one I prefer though, so I wouldn't shy away from saving $40 by picking up the older Nimbus in the sales.

The Asics Superblast 3 is one of the better running shoes I've tested in 2026, but this deal on the Superblast 2 is still very tempting. It's a max-cushioned sneaker that feels great at almost any pace, and you can save $50 on a couple of colors of the shoe in the Amazon sale right now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For every field, circuits for the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, and for the permanent outside characteristic 2, need more than m^(c (log m)^(1/3)) gates for all large m.
  • Sources indicate that the result was discovered by an internal research Claude model.
  • Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For every field, circuits for the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, and for the permanent outside characteristic 2, need more than m^(c (log m)^(1/3)) gates for all large m. The same holds for approximating circuits. So VP is a proper subset of VNP, and VNP is not contained in the closure of VP. This does not settle P vs NP.

Sources indicate that the result was discovered by an internal research Claude model. This folder holds the paper and its Lean 4 formalization. Both were written by AI models, and no human mathematician has checked the proof.

Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.

In a recent development, paper.pdf: VP ≠ VNP over every field, by Claude (Anthropic). The full proof is its appendix.

It has been revealed that 1. Read the statement. Statement.lean states all of the above and imports only Mathlib. Lean checks the proofs, but no machine checks that this file says what is claimed. Appendix Q of paper.pdf lists the Lean counterparts of the numbered statements (Table 3) and says where they differ.

2. Check the proofs. With elan installed, in this folder:.

The build prints sorry warnings from Challenge.lean only, which states the theorems without proofs for the fuller check. The last command should name no axiom other than propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

The fuller check is the one this repository's CI runs, bash ../.github/scripts/comparator-check.sh (Linux): Comparator compares the statements with Challenge.lean and re-checks the proofs with a second, independently written kernel, nanoda.

Why Black Friday Is the Perfect Time to Start a Gym Membership

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most people are probably waiting until Jan.
  • It has been revealed that the week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit.
  • This week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a new air fryer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people are probably waiting until Jan. 1 to start getting in shape, whether they want to start fresh or absolve themselves of their perceived holiday indulgences. Every year, people start the new year by joining a gym crowded with others newly resolved to get in shape, paying full price for the privilege of waiting in a long line to use the squat rack. This year, try something different: Start your gym membership during Black Friday.

It has been revealed that the week of Black Friday can deliver you a good discount on a gym membership, an empty gym, and a built-in two-month runway to turn a generic resolution into a real habit. While you're comparing deals on new tech, headphones, or smart home devices, here’s why you should also take a few minutes to scout out the gyms near you.

This week is as good a time to save of a gym membership as a new air fryer. Here are just a few examples of the offers out there right now:.

Orangetheory and F45 have various free-month and prize-entry promotions for newly introduced Black Friday sign-ups, and similar studios for Pilates, yoga, and strength training have discounted multi-month and annual packages.

Independent gyms, university rec centers, and local studios often run their own versions, from a free month tacked onto a longer commitment to waived joining fees.

In a recent development, deals vary a lot by location, so call or stop by the clubs near you and ask what's available. Then remember to always read the fine print before you sign:.

Look at the price after the promotion ends, not just the first month's rate.

Ask about fees, including joining, annual, and access fees.

Try before you buy. Many gyms offer a free trial pass. It might make sense to first visit at the time of day you'd actually go.

Recent findings suggest that be honest about distance. The best gym is the one you'll actually walk into, so pick one that's close to home or work.

Gyms also run sales around Upcoming Year's, so a good Black Friday offer isn't the only deal you'll see. Even still, the savings aren't the only reason to go now.

December is reliably the quietest stretch of the gym year: People are busy with holiday travel and work deadlines, and many tell themselves they'll "start fresh in January." That means open benches, free treadmills, and staff who have time to show you how a machine works.

It has been revealed that that's a gift for any gym-goer, but especially if you're new. Learning your way around a gym is much less intimidating when it's empty. You can figure out the equipment, make your mistakes in peace, and build a routine before the January crowds arrive. Plus, this time of year is a perfect window to set and achieve a winnable goal.

From Black Friday to New Year's Day is about five weeks. By the time the January rush hits its peak and settles into its usual patterns, you could be eight weeks into a new routine. And as my colleague Beth Skwarecki explains, you really can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Beginners tend to see the fastest gains of their lifting lives in the first couple of months.

Recent findings suggest that prefer running? I know I do, and luckily, a couch-to-5K initiative works the same way. Most programs run about nine weeks and build you up gradually from short run-walk intervals. Start the week after Black Friday and you'll be running for a solid stretch by early January, and you'll be well on your way to 30 minutes at a stretch by the end of the month. By the time your Latest Year's resolution friends are just starting, you'll already be a few runs in.

This is also the season when many workplaces and health plans wrap up their open enrollment periods, which makes it a smart time to check what wellness perks you already have. Before you pay full price for anything, look into:.

Workplace wellness programs, which sometimes offer gym reimbursements, discounted memberships or fitness stipends.

Health insurance perks, since some plans include gym memberships or discounts.

According to recent reports, HSA and FSA rules, where general gym memberships usually don't qualify, but some medically recommended programs may. Also check any year-end deadlines for money you'd otherwise lose.

Corporate and employer discounts, which many large gyms offer on top of regular promotions.

Stack a workplace benefit on top of a holiday sale, and your cost per workout can drop considerably—well before Latest Year's resolution time arrives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has called Jensen Huang to a public hearing at 10am on Thursday, 3 December, according to a notice. The hearing will come less than two weeks after Nvidia’s board reinstated him as chief executive, Politico reported.

It has been revealed that huang had agreed to testify before his return. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on whether his looks have changed, Politico’s Jasper Goodman reported.

Lawmakers from both parties criticised the board’s decision on Monday. Several remarked it made it more urgent to pass tighter controls on chip exports to China.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s board remarked in its announcement that it relied on input from senior levels of the US government. On that basis, it said Huang’s return poses no national security risk. Senator John Cornyn of Texas asked what that was based on.

Recent findings suggest that no national security risk? Based on what?

— Senator John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn) November 23, 2026.

Brian Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the reports about Huang “extremely concerning” on X. In a video posted minutes after the announcement, he stated Huang still owes Congress answers under oath. A committee spokesperson told Politico the committee still expects Huang’s closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December to go ahead.

“The American people deserve answers on Mr. Huang’s relationship with this potential Chinese intelligence asset,” Mast stated.

As Chairman of the @HouseForeignGOP, export controls on our most advanced AI chips has been a top priority. The reports of Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese intelligence asset and the smuggling of our most advanced technology to China is extremely concerning.

The American people deserve answers.

— Rep. Brian Mast (@RepBrianMast) November 23, 2026.

Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said Nvidia should have moved on without Huang, Reuters reported.

“Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy,” Bacon noted.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement that the administration’s role in Huang’s return revealed Congress must act.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer stated.

It has been revealed that representative Raja Krishnamoorthi called the decision “outrageous” on X. He said Trump’s assurances could not be taken at face value, citing a $25m donation from Nvidia to Trump’s ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public hearing, he wrote.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang is outrageous. We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation.

Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom.

Sources indicate that huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him. https://t.co/9d2XnHNxtV.

— Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (@CongressmanRaja) November 23, 2026.

Representative Debbie Dingell called the decision irresponsible, as Congress has not yet heard from Huang. Representative Richard Neal mentioned the board’s reference to “input from senior levels” was one of many reasons Congress needs answers, Reuters reported. Senator Elizabeth Warren had already called the move “reckless”.

Senator Ruben Gallego went further. He wrote on X that Trump was selling out national security to keep the stock market high.

The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom.

— Ruben Gallego (@RubenGallego) November 23, 2026.

Huang’s return is likely to affect his legal representation before Congress, Semafor reported. The administration might also push back on the oversight looks, it stated.

Industry observers note that leaders in both parties are leaning towards using the coming defence bill to close gaps in chip export policy, Semafor reported. Mast is among those pushing to attach export control bills to the National Defense Authorization Act, according to Politico.

Trump told CNBC on Monday that he did not think the board would have brought Huang back without him. The White House did not respond to Semafor’s request for comment.
