Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

In a recent development, AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

According to recent reports, an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

In a recent development, finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Sources indicate that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

According to recent reports, there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

It has been revealed that but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

Industry observers note that we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

It has been revealed that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky rapidly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

In a recent development, to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a recent development, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Sources indicate that though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the organization’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Sources indicate that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

In a recent development, using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In a recent development, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

In a recent development, consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its owners because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted aims for achieving long-term objectives.

Recent findings suggest that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the manufacturer judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Industry observers note that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Recent findings suggest that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind’s illustration for its research on AI-discovered quantum algorithms.

Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents to find more efficient quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems. Each result was proved correct in the Lean theorem prover, because the circuits are too large to test on today’s computers.

In a recent development, google DeepMind states teams of AI agents have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design. The agents, running on Gemini 4, proved each result correct with Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs, the lab remarked on Monday.

Industry observers note that the proofs matter because the circuits are too big to test. They need thousands of qubits, far beyond what classical computers can simulate or today’s quantum chips can run.

Industry observers note that the biggest gain came in a fusion problem. The agents cut the cost of a quantum calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel by 11.8 times, and its memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, DeepMind states.

According to recent reports, they also made a simulation of a light-sensitive molecule about eight times cheaper. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, the cost fell 2.5 times. A widely used maths routine became more than 290 times cheaper.

It has been revealed that separate agent teams worked on each problem and shared verified ideas in a common notebook. Every four hours, they met in a virtual conference to debate and compare approaches. The work, with Google Quantum AI, used Google’s most powerful model, Gemini 4 Carbon.

According to recent reports, an outside checker re-ran every proof so agents could not game the tests, according to the paper. That risk is real: in a DeepMind experiment in September, 14% of agents cheated on Lean maths problems.

DeepMind cautions that the simulations would still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer. It has open-sourced its Lean library and results, building on its 2024 work to trim quantum circuits with AlphaTensor-Quantum. Earlier this month, its agents also proved Signal’s encryption code correct, and Google Quantum AI tested a key quantum effect on up to 105 qubits.

The Last Time the Fed Kept Raising Rates, the S&P 500 Fell 25%. History Says Long-Term Investors Still Came Out Ahead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure is the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index.
  • This has forced the central bank's hand, as it's an institution tasked with controlling rising prices across the economy.
  • In a recent development, stock market investors aren't exactly encouraged by this trend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Neil Patel – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:18PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure is the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index. A 2% reading is the long-run target. Even excluding food and energy, the U.S. has been running well above that for five years.

This has forced the central bank's hand, as it's an institution tasked with controlling rising prices across the economy. It raised the fed funds rate 25 basis points in September. The market is certain another hike is in store next month. The big banks believe the benchmark rate will continue to rise in early 2027.

In a recent development, stock market investors aren't exactly encouraged by this trend. The last time the Fed kept raising rates, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +4.73%) fell 25%. You might hesitate to put money to work right now.

It's better to be bullish, though. History says long-term investors still come out ahead.

In a recent development, in March 2022, the Fed launched its previous tightening campaign. From February 2022 to August 2023, it lifted the upper end of its target range from 0.25% to 5.50%.

It has been revealed that inflation forced the move. The PCE price index climbed 6.8% year over year in June 2022, its fastest pace since 1982. The central bank had held rates near zero for almost two years following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. It had to play catch-up.

In a recent development, higher rates can squeeze stocks in multiple ways. They raise borrowing costs for companies, which can pressure capital investments. And they make bonds and cash look more attractive by comparison, weighing on valuations.

Wall Street didn't take it well. From its January 2022 high to its October 2022 low, the S&P 500 index shed 25%. The last bear market saw roughly a quarter of the market's value vanish in about nine months.

According to recent reports, many investors might have missed this detail. Stocks bottomed even as the Fed still had months of rate hikes ahead. Its final increase didn't come until July 2023. The market, a forward-looking machine, started climbing long before borrowing costs stopped rising.

Betting on the recovery still demanded patience from investors. The benchmark didn't close above its January 2022 high until Jan. 19, 2024. It took two years just to get back to even.

The momentum didn't let up. The S&P 500 presently sits 50% above its 2022 peak (as of Nov. 19), even though it's 8% below its record. That's also after the Fed resumed hiking in September and with the latest meeting minutes showing that almost all officials expect additional increases.

Run the numbers. If you invested $10,000 in the S&P 500 at its January 2022 high, you watched it shrink to about $7,500 by that October. If you had steady hands, it would be worth roughly $15,000 today, before dividends.

Industry observers note that the investor who sold near the bottom locked in a $2,500 loss, which would have relieved the pain. A second, harder decision was next. You had to figure out when to get back in. It's easier said than done. And few people buy confidently while panic-filled headlines are widespread.

Recent findings suggest that that's the trap of market timing. You have to be right twice. Selling at the start of a hiking cycle feels prudent to cut losses. But the last cycle demonstrated it was a costly mistake.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, anyone who kept investing through the slump was fine. From its October 2022 low, the index has roughly doubled.

Industry observers note that none of this guarantees a repeat performance. Today's inflation is tied partly to an energy shock, and rates could climb further than markets expect. There's no rule saying stocks can't fall hard again. Investors need to accept that possibility.

A 25% drawdown definitely hurts, even when history proves it's temporary. But having a five-year-plus horizon changes the math. The goal is to stay invested long enough for corporate earnings growth, the key fundamental tailwind, to do the heavy lifting. The goal isn't to predict the Fed's next move. Nobody does that consistently.

In a recent development, rate hikes are back, and the playbook hasn't changed. Time in the market beats timing the market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic has opened Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in public beta, letting it scan for misuse across many Claude requests while companies keep their data in their own cloud storage. It answers enterprise pushback over the 30-day retention Anthropic introduced with Fable 5.

Anthropic has opened a upcoming safety system for business users of Claude in a public beta, the organization mentioned on Monday. Called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), it looks for misuse without Anthropic keeping any of their data.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s basic filters check each request on its own. But it notes serious attacks are often split into many small requests that each look harmless. Its September threat report told of AI agents that split one attack on about 50 groups into small tasks.

Industry observers note that catching that needs stored records, so Anthropic began keeping data for 30 days when it debuted Fable 5. Many tightly regulated firms balked. With EFS, prompts and replies go to the customer’s own Amazon or Google cloud account instead, locked so not even the customer can read them.

Anthropic’s software scans that data, but no one at Anthropic or the cloud firm sees it, and it is never used for training. When the system spots a risk, it opens a “safety case.” The customer’s security team must look into it within seven days, or risk losing access.

“We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection,” stated Munish Kumar Sharma, chief information security officer at Wells Fargo.

More than 100 customers helped build EFS, Anthropic says, including Bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe. It is free, though customers pay their cloud firm for storage. OpenAI previewed a similar system, Private Safety Processing, in August.

Freeing the iPod Nano 5G

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viktorkrapivin

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit.
  • I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit.
  • It has been revealed that existing DFU exploits, including q3kâs wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit. Whether the same approach would work on the 5G was still an open question.

I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit. My motivation was simple: an up-to-date music player without an internet connection. I built a fully untethered boot chain that loads Rockbox from the nano 5Gâs NAND, with no computer or button sequence needed after installation. I also found a way to make the existing exploit fully untethered on the nano 7G, and likely the 6G too.

It has been revealed that existing DFU exploits, including q3kâs wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time. I used wInd3x to explore the device and develop a convenient, fully untethered exploit. The firmware details below refer to the latest nano 5G firmware, 1.0.2 (34A20020).

In a recent development, the nano 5Gâs NAND flash appears through a flash translation layer (FTL) as a logical disk with 4 KiB sectors. Its partition table separates a small private area for persistent device state, a firmware partition containing boot programs and resources, and a data volume for user files. The firmware partition has a directory of named images; the fonts live inside rsrc, a resource volume formatted as FAT16.

It has been revealed that the original ipod_sun chain combines a resource-validation bypass with a font-parser vulnerability. Appleâs firmware directory identifies the normal operating system as osos, the disk-mode program as disk, and the resource image containing fonts as rsrc. The disk-mode boot path does not request the resource signature check used by normal OS boot.

According to recent reports, swapping the disk and osos directory entries exploits that difference: selecting disk mode now introduces Appleâs regular OS under the disk-mode policy. The OS still reads its fonts, but the bootloader has not required a valid signature for the modified resource image.

The font then triggers CVE-2010-1797, the FreeType CFF stack-overflow vulnerability also known through the star exploit. A malformed font program corrupts the parserâs stack and redirects execution. My 5G port adapts that technique to the deviceâs font and execution context.

The swapped images remain on disk, but each restart still requires choosing disk mode with the deviceâs buttons. A normal boot selects the other entry. I wanted a better experience, with the modified font loading through the normal OS path.

The bootloader is organized into EFI-style modules stored as Portable Executable (PE) images. The module that passes execution to the next boot stage decides whether to validate rsrc. It first asks the PrivateData module for FirmwareStatus, which comes from an authenticated record in the private NAND partition.

Sources indicate that the decisive branch is below. This is reconstructed C from the reverse-engineered routine, with unrelated fuse handling and protocol setup omitted.

A value of 2 returns success before the resource-validation query. Bit 0 must remain clear: it is checked first, so 3 would reject the boot attempt. Tracing the restore OS indicates that it sets the status to 1 during firmware transfer and clears it to 0 at the end. This suggests an upgrade-in-progress guard that prevents booting an incomplete installation.

Appleâs resource-mount path writes status 2 only on the first successful boot, after rsrc has passed signature verification. My hypothesis is that this avoids repeating signature verification to shorten boot time or reduce energy use.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second bypass. Instead of disguising the normal OS as disk mode, I can leave the firmware directory alone and supply a valid private record with bit 1 set. The normal boot path then accepts the modified resource image, and its font delivers code execution automatically.

The record lives in the private partition, identified by MBR type 0x3e. On the 5G layout I examined, the partition begins at logical block 1, with 4 KiB blocks. The bootloader reads a 512-byte header from its start. The status-bearing format begins with the little-endian magic PRVD and has this layout:.

The integrity tag is device-specific, so creating and saving a valid PRVD record requires code execution on that iPod.

The tag is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-1 digest, encrypted with the deviceâs hardware AES UID key, selected through key slot 2. It authenticates the private header, but as the authentication is constructed on device we can falsify it if we have code execution.

Sources indicate that to inspect and update the private partition, I adapted emCORE, an older framework from freemyipodâs earlier iPod exploitation and boot work. It provided an existing USB-controlled environment to extend for the 5G.

In a recent development, I wrote the nano 5G NAND driver and integrated it into emCORE alongside the flash translation layer (FTL) and hardware AES access. Iâll cover the flash memory sequencer subsystem (FMSS), which enables NAND writes, in a future post. The FTL presents logical sectors over physical flash; it is the layer through which I read and write the private record and install the modified font.

The private-status tool verifies the existing header and tag, constructs the updated record, and obtains its new tag from the device. It rechecks the partition table and header before writing, then flushes the write and reads it back. The tool writes a complete 4 KiB logical sector even though the bootloader only consumes the smaller header. This works on nano 5G hardware.

Recent findings suggest that once the private record and modified font are installed, they remain in NAND across restarts. emCORE and the host computer are needed for the installation workflow, not for each subsequent boot.

Recent findings suggest that reaching the font parser automatically solved persistence. The next constraint was fitting something useful inside the font. I wanted it to load Rockbox from storage, so the payload needed a NAND driver, a flash translation layer, a filesystem reader, and enough startup code to hand off reliably.

To fit, I compiled with size and link-time optimizations and had the linker remove unused sections. The Rockbox kernel is stored on the deviceâs FAT32 partition and can be easily updated.

According to recent reports, code execution initially arrives in a damaged FreeType call frame. The stack has been corrupted, and Appleâs OS has left interrupts, DMA controllers, timers, caches, and address translation configured for its own use. Jumping straight into a large C program would carry that state into storage initialization.

I split the bootstrap into two images. The first is the 808-byte assembly stub at 0x22050000. Its job is to leave the parser context: mask IRQs and FIQs, switch to a private stack, stop inherited timer activity, quiesce DMA and clock domains, and clean up caches and the MMU before entering the main payload. It replaces the damaged stack and then jumps to the Rockbox kernel loader.

According to recent reports, the second image is the main loader at 0x22060000. Its entry code disables the watchdog before starting the NAND scan, installs its own stack, and clears the uninitialized-data area before calling C. The watchdog matters because reconstructing the logical flash mapping can take several seconds; a reset in the middle would stop the boot before it ever found Rockbox.

In a recent development, this separation keeps the most fragile stage small. The assembly stub establishes a controlled execution environment; the main payload can then do the more substantial storage work in freestanding C.

According to recent reports, at the hardware level, the NAND driver uses FMSS, a programmable microcontroller, to communicate with the NAND chips. lemonjesusâs earlier work on the S5L8702 sequencer, published as S5L8702-FMISS-Tools, documents its instruction set and provides tools for inspecting and building bytecode. That research is key prior work for understanding this part of the storage hardware; my work here uses the sequencer to read NAND as part of the nano 5G boot path.

The loader first checks that the microsecond timer used for driver timeouts is running. It then initializes the read-only NAND and FTL stack, mounts the FAT filesystem, and opens /.rockbox/rockbox.ipod. The core sequence follows the Rockbox bootloaderâs own file-loading path:.

Recent findings suggest that the file loader checks the Rockbox model identifier and checksum, then leaves the executable image at 0x08000000. The final handoff keeps interrupts masked, cleans and invalidates caches, drains pending writes, and branches to that address. Rockboxâs startup code takes over from there. If storage, mounting, or image loading fails, the payload shows the failing stage on the LCD and stops.

On my nano 5G, the result is a cold, battery-powered boot straight into Rockbox, with no USB connection and no disk-mode button sequence. The PRVD partition setting skips rsrc validation and, when combined with the star exploit, enables untethered boot straight into Rockbox. The main constraint is that the font payload is limited to 27,874 bytes. Installation and restoration procedures, along with the reverse-engineering notes and build details, are in the nano5g_bootstub and nano5g_emCORE repositories below.

I have confirmed that the private-data partition works the same way on the nano 7G, which suggests the method will likely work on the 6G too. I initiative to get the nano 4G and 5G Rockbox ports into good shape before applying this method to the 6G and 7G.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most key iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

According to recent reports, have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

Industry observers note that I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a upcoming volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk's company is facing two newly introduced lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.
  • Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent company of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X.
  • According to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk's company is facing two newly introduced lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.

Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent company of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X. Both states allege that the company failed to implement adequate safeguards against the creation of nonconsensual sexual images, including child sexual abuse material.

According to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S. states over the controversy, although several attorneys general have already investigated Grok's image-generation features.

The lawsuits also raise a broader concern for anyone who shares photos online. As AI image generators become more realistic and accessible, how much control do people actually have over what others can create using their pictures?

Here's what happened, what the lawsuits allege and what it could mean for Grok consumers.

The lawsuits focus on Grok's ability to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

Sources indicate that grok includes image-generation and editing features that can transform an uploaded photo using text instructions. According to the states, owners exploited these capabilities to create explicit or partially nude images of real people without their knowledge or consent.

The complaints specifically point to Grok's controversial "spicy mode," which the states say enabled the generation of sexual content without sufficient protections.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield argue that the manufacturer promoted the safety of its tools while failing to prevent the creation and distribution of harmful images.

The states accuse SpaceX of violating consumer protection laws and are seeking financial penalties, damages and court orders requiring the company to stop the alleged violations.

These are allegations in civil lawsuits, not findings of wrongdoing by a court.

One of the most alarming figures cited in the lawsuits comes from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH).

The organization estimated that between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok generated and posted approximately 3 million sexualized images on X, including around 23,000 images that appeared to depict children.

That works out to roughly 190 sexualized images every minute over the study period.

Sources indicate that the figures are estimates from the organization's research rather than a confirmed count of illegal images. Nevertheless, the scale described in the study has become a central part of the states' allegations.

The Virginia Attorney General's Office also alleges that nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified in the study remained publicly accessible on X at least a week after they were identified.

In a recent development, yes. In January 2026, xAI announced restrictions on Grok's image-editing capabilities, including measures intended to prevent customers from generating images of real people in revealing clothing where doing so would be illegal.

However, subsequent reporting raised questions about whether the changes were effective.

In February, Reuters found that Grok could still generate sexualized images of people even when prompts explicitly stated that the subjects had not consented.

According to recent reports, the new lawsuits argue that the company's safeguards were inadequate and that its public assurances about user safety were misleading. The company has separately taken legal action against individuals it alleges misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

For most people, the concern goes beyond generating inappropriate AI images.

The lawsuits highlight a growing problem with generative AI: someone may be able to use a photograph of another person to produce realistic fabricated content without that person's permission.

Recent findings suggest that an AI-generated image does not have to depict something that actually happened to cause harm. A convincing fake can be copied, shared or used to harass someone, especially when it circulates on a major social media platform.

The risk is particularly concerning for parents whose children's photos may be publicly accessible online. These lawsuits do not mean that every Grok user has had their photos manipulated, nor do they establish that simply uploading a photo to X causes Grok to generate an explicit image.

Still, they are a reminder that publicly available images can be vulnerable to misuse by people with access to powerful AI editing tools.

Recent findings suggest that people concerned about this risk can review the visibility of their social media accounts, limit public sharing of sensitive images and report manipulated content when they encounter it. Such precautions cannot eliminate the possibility of misuse, especially when a photograph has already been copied or circulated elsewhere.

In a recent development, both states are seeking penalties and court orders aimed at stopping the alleged unlawful conduct. The courts have not yet determined whether SpaceX violated either state's consumer protection laws.

The company also faces more than a dozen lawsuits from individuals who allege that Grok was used to create nonconsensual sexual images of them.

The outcome of the lawsuit could help determine how much responsibility AI companies bear when their tools are used to create harmful images of real people.

But for now, the Grok lawsuits underscore a concern that extends to AI image generation as it has become remarkably powerful, but protecting the people whose likenesses appear in those images remains an unresolved challenge.

#154060. Tech Report: AI coding agents used firms’ own code under 60% of the time, study finds

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (962 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: AI coding agents used firms’ own code under 60% of the time, study finds

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrei Manolache, CEO and co-founder of DesignVerse.
  • Recent findings suggest that AI coding agents without company context used an organisation’s own approved code in fewer than six tasks in ten.
  • The AI Coding Drift Report, published today, tested agents on 15 private enterprise codebases in aviation, banking, defence, software services and consultancy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrei Manolache, CEO and co-founder of DesignVerse.

Recent findings suggest that AI coding agents without company context used an organisation’s own approved code in fewer than six tasks in ten. That is the main finding of upcoming research from DesignVerse, a Bucharest-based enterprise AI startup. The rest of the time, the agents invented components or swapped in public ones. Engineers then had to find and fix them by hand.

The AI Coding Drift Report, published today, tested agents on 15 private enterprise codebases in aviation, banking, defence, software services and consultancy. Each system is 15 to 20 years old and has more than a million lines of code. A team of about 20 engineers looks after each one. Most are written in Ada, C++ or COBOL.

Industry observers note that the report compared two of the most widely used coding agents, anonymised as Agent A and Agent B, with DesignVerse’s own context-engineered system. The two agents ran in their standard setup with full repository access, but no custom rules or extra tech giant context, Andrei Manolache, DesignVerse’s CEO and co-founder, told TNW. That is how most teams use them, he noted.

DesignVerse’s system ran on its own model. Before each call, it pulled the relevant parts of the client’s code and engineering and business documents.

According to recent reports, “So this isn’t a comparison of the same model with and without context. It’s a comparison between the typical coding-agent setup available to engineering teams today and a context-engineered alternative,” Manolache said.

In a recent development, the unmanaged agents used the organisation’s own internal software components 55% to 59% of the time. DesignVerse’s system did so 92% of the time. A task failed if the agent invented an interface or library, or picked a public one when an internal one existed.

Recent findings suggest that given the same task repeatedly, the unmanaged agents gave the same answer 61% to 69% of the time. DesignVerse’s system did so 97% of the time. There were about ten tasks per codebase, and up to 40, from small refactors and unit tests to changes across several systems. Each was the kind of change that could take an engineer around 100 hours, Manolache remarked.

Without a context layer, agents read a median of ten tokens for every token of accepted code. On one client’s legacy system, measured outside the main benchmark, the ratio reached 150 to one.

DesignVerse’s team and the clients’ own engineers scored the results together, against the rubric published in the report. Every setup got the same tasks, prompts, tool access, time limits and grading. The one difference was the context layer.

“It’s a fair challenge. We sell the system, so we have an obvious interest in the outcome. That’s precisely why we made the methodology public and reproducible. We don’t think anyone should have to take our word for it,” Manolache remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the 15 organisations were already working with or evaluating DesignVerse, which the report discloses. That gave it access to private, million-line systems missing from public benchmarks, he stated. The company is not naming them because of confidentiality agreements. The report includes a two-week test any team can run on its own code, with any model, without DesignVerse.

Recent findings suggest that the cost figure comes from one client’s product over 12 months, not from the benchmark. Without a context layer, the work took nine developers and 9,600 hours, Manolache remarked. With one, it took five developers and 4,000 hours, a 58% cut.

DesignVerse values the 5,600 hours freed at about $882,000. It used a blended rate of $157.50 an hour, taken from the client’s $1.5m labour bill. At $120 an hour the figure would be about $672,000, and at $200 about $1.12m. It leaves out platform, licensing and token costs, and the cost of building the context layer. Nobody lost their job, he stated: the hours went to the backlog.

“If companies are paying for AI to write code, only to pay their engineers to fix it afterwards, they need to ask some serious questions about the return on that investment,” Manolache said in the release.

Sources indicate that in Qodo’s 2026 State of AI Code Quality report, 90% of US engineering leaders mentioned they were confident reporting AI’s impact to their board, but only 45% could trace AI activity to the code it produced. Gartner has warned about rising AI coding costs.

According to recent reports, to work in a regulated industry, a general US model needs three things, Manolache remarked. It needs the firm’s context, has to run under the company’s control and must fit how it builds software. Most of that knowledge is not in any model’s training data, he said. He expects smaller, specialised models with a context layer the company owns. Otherwise, he said, a company could spend $100m on infrastructure for 50 engineers.

In a recent development, “My message to European companies is simple: don’t wait for a US model to solve your sovereignty problem. Build the layer of intelligence and knowledge that you should own. The model underneath should be interchangeable. And that remains true whether you work with us or not,” he noted.

The fight between coding tools has moved beyond the models. DeepSeek’s Super-Agent reads team chats to get its context.

The report ends with five recommendations. DesignVerse raised a $5.5 million seed round in May, led by Begin Capital and Gapminder VC. It said then that it had rebuilt a 15-year-old EUROCONTROL application in just over a month, against an estimated six months.

Nvidia Stock Adds $950 Billion in a Day as Jensen Huang Returns. Here's What Analysts Now Project

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) shares closed at $165.05 on Monday, surging 31% from Friday's $125.53, after the company said its board had reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director.
  • Recent findings suggest that the rally recovered most of the losses the stock incurred after Huang stepped down.
  • 22 to bring Huang back, Nvidia unveiled the following morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 23, 2026 at 4:18PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) shares closed at $165.05 on Monday, surging 31% from Friday's $125.53, after the company said its board had reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director. The gain added about $950 billion to Nvidia's market value, which rose to about $3.98 trillion.

Recent findings suggest that the rally recovered most of the losses the stock incurred after Huang stepped down. Nvidia disclosed on Nov. 12 that the board had accepted his resignation the day before and named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO. The stock closed at $173.73 on Nov. 11 and fell 28% over the next seven trading days. Monday's close is still 5% below that level and 31% below the all-time closing high of $239.24 set on Oct. 6.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Nvidia.

The board voted unanimously on Nov. 22 to bring Huang back, Nvidia unveiled the following morning. It said it was "satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia" after a series of meetings with him.

The board also said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and, based on that input, is confident Huang's return "poses no national security risk." Harvey Jones, who became chair when Huang resigned, stays in that role, and Kress stays on as CFO.

"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang stated in the release.

Several analysts raised their views within hours. Oppenheimer upgraded the stock to outperform with a $250 price target, calling Huang's return "a win for AI and a win for investors." StoneX upgraded it to buy with a $270 target. Citi raised its target to $240 from $225 and said the move removes the "key overhang" from the CEO change. BMO Capital kept its outperform rating and $240 target.

Bernstein also upgraded the stock to outperform. It had downgraded Nvidia 11 days earlier and cut its price target in half when Huang's exit looked likely.

Recent findings suggest that the same press release that lauds Huang's return lists the remaining open problems. In light of reporting that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," a committee of independent directors is investigating with outside counsel, and the board noted that investigation "will proceed to conclusion." Huang said he supports it.

Nvidia also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors, is searching for its first chief compliance officer, and remarked it "will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.".

Some analysts flagged those concerns on Monday. Bernstein kept its $200 target even after the upgrade, saying "this whole mess has brought up some legitimate questions" and will leave some overhangs in place. Goldman Sachs, which rates the stock a buy, mentioned Nvidia's operations in certain jurisdictions could face more scrutiny. It also questioned whether Nvidia will keep striking large investment deals with partners at the same scale. Baird, which rates the stock neutral with a $200 target, called the combination of Huang's return and strict limits on AI chip access a worst-case scenario for China and said medium-term revenue uncertainty remains.

Only two of those price targets, StoneX's $270 and Oppenheimer's $250, sit above the stock's all-time closing high. Bernstein's and Baird's $200 targets are about 21% above Monday's close.

Recent findings suggest that monday removed perhaps the biggest single risk for Nvidia (the need to operate without the founder who built it), but it didn't settle the question of why he left. The internal investigation, the government inquiries, and the fresh compliance structure could still change how Nvidia does business, especially in China.

So is Nvidia a buy? For long-term investors who can live with big swings, yes, but in measured amounts. The stock still trades 31% below its October level with its founder back in charge, and every price target cited here, from $200 to $270, sits above Monday's close. Buyers should expect more volatility until the investigation's findings are known, which matters for semiconductor stocks and AI stocks more broadly, too. Anyone who needs certainty about the inquiries can wait for those results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

Industry News: MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the biggest problem with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the biggest problem with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker claims it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

Sources indicate that the MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

It has been revealed that anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also swiftly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Sources indicate that qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I remarked in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

10 stocks we like better than Bitcoin ›.

Recent findings suggest that leading cryptocurrency Bitcoin (BTC +0.17%) is down 30% since the start of the year. Last week, it also briefly fell below $60,000 as market sentiment soured amid concerning developments at Nvidia, which dragged the overall stock market down.

Bitcoin, which has often followed the movements of the broader market, has shown that it's no safer an option than other high-risk investments. With there being plenty of uncertainty still ahead and a potential for more rate hikes, could Bitcoin fall to $50,000 or lower before the end of the year?

Government regulation can play a key role in the acceptance and growth of cryptocurrency. It's worth noting, then, that since the midterm elections took place earlier this month, Bitcoin's value has dropped immensely. From around $77,000 before the midterm elections took place to around $61,000 now, the cryptocurrency's value has already fallen by more than 20% since then.

In a recent development, investors may be concerned that, even with a seemingly pro-crypto government, significant reform couldn't take place. The Clarity Act, which would establish clear rules for crypto trading, failed to pass and may now be even less likely under a Democratic-controlled Congress.

To make matters worse, there's the potential for more rate hikes ahead. Next month, it appears all but certain that there will be at least a 25-basis-point hike, and an outside chance that rates could go up by 50 basis points. Interest rate hikes are bad news for speculative investments such as crypto. A big rate increase could indeed give Bitcoin a further push down in value.

CRYPTO · As of 9:16 PM ET 11/23/26.

Sources indicate that bitcoin is a highly speculative investment, and a lot depends on investor sentiment. Unfortunately, the appetite for risk lessens as interest rates rise. And without a catalyst on the horizon to increase crypto adoption, I don't see why things might turn around anytime soon.

It has been revealed that instead, it appears more likely that the leading cryptocurrency will continue to fall in value as investors grow more concerned about the broader markets. Bitcoin could fall to $50,000 or lower this year, depending on the extent of interest rate increases. However, even if they don't increase significantly, with plenty of concerns about the economy these days, there may be more investors looking to cash out of crypto than those looking to start a position in it.

I expect Bitcoin to fall below $50,000; it's just a matter of how quickly it happens.

Anthropic is launching a newly introduced tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

Claude Ship is a newly introduced product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic claims. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic indicates.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the fresh /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic states.

It has been revealed that you can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI.
  • Also: I checked Gemini’s upcoming Memory summary to see what it knew about me.
  • It has been revealed that in a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback.

Also: I checked Gemini’s upcoming Memory summary to see what it knew about me.

It has been revealed that in a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes.

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google stated in an announcement shared to Gemini owners via email.

Industry observers note that here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both fresh settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

Sources indicate that almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history.

ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”.

Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027.

According to recent reports, in all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction.
